However, one of the most important connections of all that JOLO made was with the people who ran Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund.
Now, quick side note, what the hell is a sovereign wealth fund?
Well, it's essentially a giant pool of money that's controlled by a nation's government.

Most commonly, they're used by countries that are dependent on a single resource, like countries in the Middle East whose economies are highly dependent on oil, and they use these funds to diversify their money into other assets and investments.
However, these sovereign wealth funds have so much cash and are mostly unregulated with very little transparency or oversight.
And that's why they would be crucial for Jolo's future schemes.
But first, after essentially going on a networking tour around the Middle East, Jolo returned to university to graduate.
And it was at that point Jolo set up his own company, which he called the Winton Group.
He told friends that he'd chosen the name because he was going to Winton's of money.
Seriously.
The basic idea behind the company was that he'd broker deals between Middle Eastern investors who wanted to get involved in projects in Malaysia.

So Jolo got luxurious offices for this new company in the famous Patronus Towers, which he couldn't really afford, but he managed to arrange a loan from a local bank because Jolo knew it was important to give off the perception this was a serious and successful business.
Of course, he now needed some actual clients.
And luckily for Jolo, all of his networking with wealthy elites was about to start paying off in a very major way.
One of Jolo's best friends from his days at Haro was Reza Aziz, who was the stepson of a prominent Malaysian government official called Najib Razak.

In fact, by the time Jolo had started his company up, Najib had become Deputy Prime Minister of Malaysia, which obviously meant he had a lot of power, and Jolo knew there could be some huge advantages for him if he could get inside Najib's inner circle.
Of course, just being good friends with Najib's stepson wasn't enough by itself.
Jolo had to prove his value.
And that's when Jolo heard that Malaysia was looking for partners to develop a giant construction project.
The idea for it was basically to build a financial and lifestyle centre similar to Singapore.
But they needed investors.
Jolo saw an opportunity here.
Using the wealthy connections he'd made in the Middle East, he was able to broker a deal where they would invest in Malaysia's construction project.
But here's the crucial part.
but Jolo let Najib, Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister, take all the credit for the deal, despite not having to do any of the work.
This massively boosted Najib's popularity with the Malaysian people, as he was now seen as a politician who could attract big investments and help propel Malaysia forward.
In fact, this popularity he gained was one of the factors in helping him become Prime Minister of Malaysia in 2009.
Now Jolo's original business model was that he'd simply get a fee for brokering these kinds of deals, but he didn't actually get a fee for this construction project.
Instead, Jolo got something better.
He was now loved by Najib, who was extremely grateful to Jolo.
And so, in 2009 when Najib became Prime Minister of Malaysia, it meant Jolo, who at this point was just 27 years old, now had the ear of the most powerful man in the country.
And Jolo didn't stop there, he tried to fully embed himself into Najib's family.
He bought Najib's wife expensive jewellery, and even paid for Najib's daughter's college tuition, as well as attending her graduation ceremony.
By this point, Najib trusted Jolo fully, and And so after Najib was sworn in as Prime Minister of Malaysia, Jolo wasted no time in approaching him with an idea.
Jolo said Malaysia should create their own sovereign wealth fund, similar to the ones in the Middle East, which could be used to invest all around the world.
And so together, they set up the One Malaysia Development Berhad, or the 1MDB fund for short.
Now officially, the 1MDB fund was supposed to develop the country's economy, it would supposedly be used to invest in green energy and tourism and create high quality jobs for all Malaysians.
But Jolo explained to Najib that if he put him in charge of the fund, they could use some of the money as a war chest to fund Najib's political goals.

For example, the fund could be used for Najib to host big events, or to build affordable housing in areas where Najib hadn't received many votes in the election, as a way to get more of the country loyal to him.
Jolo had the Malaysian Prime Minister in the palm of his hand.
He'd helped Najib get elected, and now he was proposing a deal to help Najib consolidate power even further.
To Najib, the whole idea seemed like a win-win.
So, Najib let Jolo run the 1MDB fund and do whatever he wanted with basically no oversight.
Officially, Najib had the title of the fund's chairman, whilst Jolo was simply classed as an advisor.
But in reality, Jolo controlled the whole fund, and he hired people he knew well as staff who were blindly loyal to him.
Meaning, Jolo essentially had full control over what to do with Malaysia's billion dollar fund.
Within a couple of months, Jolo had found the first deal for the 1MDB fund to invest in.
Using connections Jolo had made in Saudi Arabia, he'd arranged a joint venture with the oil company Petro Saudi.
The plan was that 1MDB would invest $1 billion into this oil project, which was basically all the money in the fund at the time.
But Jolo got permission from Najib to transfer the money from 1MDB's account, since Najib was happy to trust Jolo fully.

However, since Jolo was fully in charge of the money, he actually only sent $300 million to the joint venture account with Petro Saudi, whilst the remaining $700 million went to a company called Goodstar Limited, which had a bank account in Switzerland.

Jolo claimed that Goodstar Limited was a company owned by the Saudis, and said that 1MDB had to send the money to Goodstar as part of the deal, because of a debt they had to pay before the joint venture could continue.
But this wasn't true.
This Goodstar Limited was merely a shell company, and it used something called bearer shares.
Now, with normal shares in a company, they'd be registered to an individual's name, and there'd be a registry of who owns shares in the company.

However, a bearer share is a type of share where whoever holds the physical share certificate has full ownership of it, thus making it very hard to tell who really owns the company, and therefore making it very useful for frauds.
In the case of Goodstar Limited, it was later revealed that there was only one physical share, and that share was held by Jolo.
In other words, Jolo had just sent $700 million from the 1MDB fund to Goodstar Limited's bank account, and Jolo owned 100% of Goodstar Limited's.
So on paper, it seemed like 1MDB had simply invested in the Petro-Saudi joint venture as planned.
But in reality, Jolo had just paid himself $700 million.
In many ways, it was such an incredibly simple move, but it was the meticulous planning to get to this position of power in the first place that had made it possible.
From an early age, Jolo had been actively seeking the right connections, and then providing value to those connections in order to cultivate such an influential and powerful network who trusted him.

He'd identified sovereign wealth funds as a tool that could be easily exploited, and once he'd got the Malaysian Prime Minister to grant him full power of the 1MDB fund, siphoning off money for his own personal gain had been relatively straightforward.
He just had to bribe a few senior people for their silence, but that wasn't hard to do when he'd just got 700 million dollars, and had deliberately surrounded himself with loyal yes men.
And now, it was time for the real fun to begin.

Jolo had successfully taken money from the Malaysian fund and funneled it to Swiss bank accounts under the guise it was an investment, and he'd then use friends in high ranking positions to make sure nobody questioned anything.
Jolo now had hundreds of millions of dollars sat in a bank account.
This is very different to most rich people whose wealth is heavily tied up in companies' stock or investments, but for Jolo it was all available to spend, and he could do whatever he wanted with it.
So, with all of this stolen money, Jolo began living a life of luxury.
He went on a spending spree of yachts, mansions and sports cars.
He even bought a big hotel in Beverly Hills.
But most nights, you'd find Jolo at an exclusive nightclub or casino.

In fact, it's reported that in the eight months between October 2009 and June 2010, Jolo and his friends spent around $85 million on private jets, alcohol, gambling and paying models and Hollywood with celebrities to party with them.
It was non-stop partying and networking.
You see, Jolo realised he could use the money from 1MDB to get close to the rich and famous, and build an even greater reputation for himself.
And thus, he put the word out in show business circles that he was happy to pay celebs over $100,000 a night to attend his parties.
Even to rich celebrities, they'd never seen anything quite like Jolo's levels of spending.
This was a whole different level of rich.
He'd lose a million dollars in a game of poker, and wouldn't seem to care.
As a result, Jolo got to meet all kinds of famous people.
For example, Jolo had fantasized about Paris Hilton since his college days, now he was regularly hanging out with her.
There's also stories of Jolo being in a Las Vegas hotel suite with Leonardo DiCaprio, surrounded by 20 Playboy bunnies.
Jolo would also buy out prestigious clubs, and then throw secret parties with friends and celebrities.
He'd give out incredibly expensive gifts, like he gave Kim Kardashian a white Ferrari for a wedding.
And he'd casually hand out designer bags that cost tens of thousands of dollars to people he'd literally just met.
And to be fair, Jello threw some of the biggest parties imaginable.
There was one particular party he threw in Vegas for his birthday that felt more like a major concert.
He had all kinds of celebrities, including Kanye West, Bradley Cooper, Robert De Niro, Michael Phelps, Kim Kardashian, Paris Hilton, and even Psy was there to sing Gangnam Style.
Oh, and he even got Britney Spears to burst out of a cake to serenade him by singing Happy Birthday.
That single night is rumoured to have cost tens of millions of dollars.
Most of the celebrities at these events were often being paid to be there.
The truth is, even the biggest stars didn't turn down hundreds of thousands of dollars to attend an event.
However, they had to admit, Jolo knew how to throw an amazing party.
And Jolo felt if his parties were successful, his own status would grow, helping him attract even more powerful people into his life.
And he was indeed getting a reputation.
When newspapers heard he'd sent 23 bottles to Lindsay Lohan's table on a night out, they dubbed him the Big Spending Malaysian, the mystery man of the city club scene.
And being surrounded by celebrities of course raised Jolo's profile further, and at one point he reportedly dated the model Miranda Kerr, who he showered with expensive gifts.
But the insanity didn't stop there.
For example, for New Year's, Jolo said he wanted to experience it twice.
So Jolo, along with some friends and celebrities, got on a private plane and flew to Sydney in Australia.
Then, after celebrating New Year's once, they flew back to Las Vegas in order to celebrate the countdown to midnight a second time in the same night.
There was also another incident where Jolo got into a bidding war with someone for a bottle of champagne, and ended up spending 2 million euros on it.
Some even started calling Jolo the Asian Great Gatsby.
But this wasn't just a reference to him throwing so many expensive, over the top parties.
It was also because Jolo seemed to observe his own parties, rather than be actively involved in them.
He'd sort of be watching on, and repeatedly checking with people if they were having a good time and enjoying it, rather than actually enjoying it himself.
Many of his guests tried to speak with him, but the conversations never seemed to get very far beyond small talk.
He actually seemed quite shy, but he clearly had an overwhelming desire to please people.
One attendee even commented that it felt fake as if we were just there to go through the motions and entertain and look cool as a group, rather than actually have fun.
It was ultimately about the pretense of wealth, prestige and status.
However, back then, if you searched for Jolo on Google, very little came up.
He was still shrouded in mystery, and people were left to speculate how he got so rich.

Some thought he was an arms dealer, or that he was descended from royalty, but despite the party playboy reputation, Jolo's closest friends nicknamed him Panda, which they said was because he was plump and cuddly.
For years, Jolo methodically cultivated relationships with the wealthiest and most powerful people on the planet.
But he also tried to learn what motivated them, and see how he could assist them.
So far, the stolen money from 1MDB had been spent on the lavish lifestyle of Jolo, along with some of it going to a political slush fund for Najib, the Malaysian Prime Minister.
But Jolo now wanted to use some of the money to start a legitimate business.
Since Jolo loved the LA lifestyle, he decided he wanted to get involved in Hollywood himself, and helped fund a production company called Red Granite Pictures.

Just like with the 1MDB fund, Jolo didn't take an official title at the company, as he didn't want records of his involvement, he preferred to be the secret money man behind it, having an active role from the shadows.

Around this time, Jolo heard that DiCaprio and Scorsese wanted to make a film about the Wolf of Wall Street, but couldn't get any of the major Hollywood studios to give them the $100 million budget they needed to make the film.
The studios said it was too risky to spend that much on a film that would get R-rated and thus a reduced audience.
So instead, Jolo's production company helped finance the movie, and gave DiCaprio and Scorsese full creative control over it.
As a result, Jolo himself was personally named in the film's credits.
Plus, when Leo won a Golden Globe for his role in the movie, he gave Jolo a shout out in his acceptance speech.

Jolo had made his first big move into Hollywood, Although, there is an obvious irony that a film like The Wolf of Wall Street would essentially be financed with stolen money, especially given the crazy partying lifestyle of the guy who funded it.
What's really interesting though, is that the real life guy that The Wolf of Wall Street is based on, Jordan Belfort, didn't trust Jolo at all.
Belfort was invited to one of Jolo's parties to celebrate them buying the rights to his story.
However, Belfort commented that something didn't seem right when he saw how overly extravagant the event was, and he said, you wouldn't spend money you work for like that, this has got to be stolen.
However, most people around Jolo were happy not to ask too many questions.
And so Jolo's company later acquired a stake in EMI Music Publishing, and he even joined the firm's advisory boards.
Between the Wolf of Wall Street movie and the EMI deal, Jolo was putting himself on the map as more than just a guy who threw big parties.
Jolo's intention now was to build a media empire that would become a legitimate profitable business.
Jolo figured eventually he might be making so much money from his media projects that he could repay the money he'd taken out of the 1MDB fund.
At the very least, Jolo knew he needed some kind of income to try and sustain his very expensive new lifestyle.
The problem was, Jolo had a compulsion to keep spending and acquiring more and more, he wanted to keep making things bigger and crazier.
And so, Jolo realised he was going to need more money fast, which meant it was time to steal some more.
Tim Leisner was head of Goldman Sachs' Asia division, and Jolo had been wooing him.
He'd arranged for a private jet to come and pick Tim up, and then taken him to a meeting with one of the richest sheiks in the world.
After giving Tim an extremely luxurious trip, Jolo explained his intentions, that he wanted Goldman Sachs to help 1MDB raise more money through bond sales.
The truth was that Jolo knew that they needed the credibility of a big Wall Street bank like Goldman Sachs to ensure the whole thing looked legitimate.
So they made a deal where Goldman Sachs would issue a bond and sell that bond to investors.
Now, investors were told that their money would help pay for power plants.
But the problem was, 1MDB had no credit rating, which made it very hard to convince people to invest.
So to make the power plant deals look better, Goldman Sachs used their credibility and paired 1MDB up with Abu Dhabi's Sovereign Wealth Fund, which had $70 billion in assets and solid credits.
Suddenly the package looked much more enticing to investors.
1MD by itself wasn't that appealing, but 1MDB, mixed with Abu Dhabi's Wealth Fund, plus with Goldman Sachs involved, that was enough for investors to buy into these bonds.
In 2012, 1MDB issued $3.5 billion in bonds through Goldman Sachs.

But as the official fund manager, Jolo used his old offshore tricks that he'd used before, and diverted $1.4 billion of that money to an offshore company registered in the British Virgin Islands which was another tax haven.
Then in 2013, 1MDB issued $3 billion more bonds through Goldman Sachs, and Jolo once again diverted some of the funds through offshore accounts.
So instead of that investor money going to power plants as advertised, Jolo had been siphoning billions of dollars into more shell companies which he controlled.
He also used some of that money to pay off everyone who had helped him pull this off, including Tim Leisner from Goldman Sachs, but the rest was Jolo's to keep.
Jolo now had billions of dollars in his offshore accounts, which allowed his crazy spending to continue.
Or if anything, get crazier.
Famous art, massive houses, and of course, yet more gambling and partying.
A big kickback also went to Najeeb, to keep the Prime Minister happy and make sure he didn't ask too many questions.
Plus, Jolo figured the money from the bond sales would help cover 1MDB's growing losses.

As for Goldman Sachs, they got around $600 million in fees and revenue, which reporters later said is around 200 times more than they'd usually make on a deal that size, indicating they knew full well something very shady was going on, but didn't ask any questions in return for a big payout.
Because remember, without Goldman Sachs getting involved, and giving their experience and reputation to the bonds, there's no way 1MDB would have been able to raise so much money.
But still, how did Jolo actually manage to siphon off billions of dollars for himself?
Firstly, one strategy was setting up bank accounts under fake company names that resembled real firms.
For example, they created a shell company called Blackrock Commodities Global Limited, which sounds just like the giant global investment company Blackrock.

So it was easy for anyone looking at the transaction to assume the money was being sent to genuine big companies so it didn't raise any obvious red flags, when in reality, they were just fake shell companies with very similar names.

Another strategy Jolo used is called layering, moving funds from one offshore bank account to another, making them look like real transactions or loans and adding layers of complexity until the original source of the funds is hidden, as it's very hard to track these offshore accounts registered in tax havens.
Jolo also had another scheme where he transferred money to trust accounts at US law firms, because client confidentiality rules in the US mean those accounts are hardly regulated.
But most importantly of all, Jolo was able to pull this off because he knew that transactions between governments attracted a lot less scrutiny from auditors and banks.
Government funds are simply not as transparent as with a regular company.
money.
As a result of all this, it's estimated in total that around 4.5 billion dollars was stolen from 1MDB.
Jolo treated the fund that was meant to help Malaysia as his personal bank account.
Of course Najib, the Malaysian Prime Minister, knew full well that 1MDB wasn't as legitimate as it seems, because he was receiving secret money from the fund for his own political ambitions.
However, Jolo had promised him that the fund would enhance relationships with the Middle East, and help bring investment and developments in Malaysia.
So Najib didn't think Jolo would literally just steal so much of the money.
Then again, giving Jolo completely unregulated power over a multi-billion dollar fund was always going to be very risky.
But still, back in Malaysia, people were starting to ask more questions about the 1MDB fund.
Like, what was happening with all that money?
Why wasn't Malaysia getting all the developments they'd been promised?
Luckily for Jolo, he still had the Prime Minister Najib on his side, so he wasn't in any danger.

Of course, the reason he had the Prime Minister on his side was that Jolo was still funneling a lot of that stolen money into financing Najib's political campaigns, including money to throw massive events or gift to charity to make Najib look good.
So 1MDB continued to burn through money, in fact it went several billions of dollars into debt.

And then in 2015, a whistleblower leaked emails to the press which included key information which would bring Jolo's schemes to light, and helped the world realise the full scale of the scam Jolo had pulled off.
The emails caused more people to dig into what was happening, and soon it started to become clearer about the scam that had taken place.
Hundreds of thousands of Malaysian citizens took to the streets to protest, and demand that Najib resign for his involvement in the 1MDB fund.
But he didn't resign.
Najib thought by the time of the next election it would have all blown over.
For Jolo, as allegations about what he'd done started to come out in the media in 2015, he realised he was going to have to go into hiding.
Jolo still had vast amounts of cash, so he'd still be able to live an extremely comfortable life, but just very isolated.
Which he hated, he didn't even like being by himself in his room.
It was also around this time that his girlfriend Miranda Kerr broke up with him.
Then in May 2018, Najib had a shock election defeat, and was voted out, with his party losing for the first time in 60 years.
In fact, it was the first regime change in Malaysia's entire history, which just shows how understandably angry the Malaysian people were at the corruption that had taken place.
Right after the election, Najib and his wife attempted to flee the country.
But protesters at the airport stopped them.
Najib claimed he was simply leaving the country for a golf trip.
But it was obvious Najib knew what was coming, now that he was no longer in power.
Shortly after this, police raided Najib's house and found $274 million worth of goods, including endless amounts of expensive jewellery, handbags, tiaras and watches, along with $28 million in cash.
It was clear Najib had been bribed.
Anti-corruption officials arrested the former Prime Minister in his mansion.

He was convicted of multiple crimes and sentenced to 12 years in prison, but he's currently appealing, claiming these were all genuine political donations, and in the meantime, he's still part of the representative arm of the government.
But as for Jolo, he was long gone.
He disappeared.
Some sources suggested he'd gone to live in China and could be residing in a villa owned by a high-ranking Chinese party official.
There's even reports he was briefly spotted at a Victoria's Secret party in Shanghai, way, suggesting he's still trying to live out the party lifestyle, albeit much more low-key than he would want.
As for Tim Leisner, the ex-Goldman Sachs manager who helped 1MDB, he pled guilty to conspiracy to commit bribery and money laundering.

Whilst Goldman Sachs tried to say it was just a few rogue employees who'd been involved in helping 1MDB launder money, in Tim's guilty plea, he said that avoiding compliance was part of the Goldman Sachs culture.
Ultimately though, the people who suffered most in all this were the Malaysian people, who were left with all the debts.
1MDB was sold as a development project that would be of benefit to all Malaysian people, but in reality, it was a cash grab, a big betrayal of the people.
Billions of dollars of Malaysian government money had been stolen and disappeared into a hidden labyrinth of offshore bank accounts and shell companies.
Even to this day, the FBI is still trying to piece everything together.
And that is money that could have genuinely helped a lot of people.
Now, it's important to state that pretty much everyone involved, from Jolo to Najeeb to Golden Saks, all deny they did anything wrong.
What is clear, is this scam was an example of how the financial system can be so easily manipulated.
Powerful people and big banks are incentivised not to ask too many questions as long as they're making money on these deals.

And perhaps most crazy of all, Jolo technically is still a free man, and you could say he got away with it, but there are many countries he can no longer visit, and he has no choice but to lay low, the exact opposite of what he wanted to do.
Reports suggest that towards the end of this, Jolo had gone from being quite a happy, relaxed guy, to being very anxious and paranoid.

And the truth is, even when he was living what many would describe as an ultimate fantasy, being so rich, partying with movie stars and models on jets and yachts, Jolo never seemed truly happy in the moment.
At least, not according to those who met him.
He seemed desperate to be liked and respected.
Which is perhaps why he kept chasing more and more money, instead of quitting while he was ahead, which ultimately led to his downfall.
Now, whilst the story of Jolo is pretty mad, I still wouldn't call him the craziest billionaire.

title: The Homeless Teen Who Created Louis Vuitton
note: Chronological family-and-company saga: rags-to-riches founder, heirs, a betrayal takeover, then modern lawsuits.
sections: Poor childhood and walk to Paris
lines: Louis Vuitton is the most valuable luxury fashion brand in the world.
Its CEO, Bernard Arnault, is also the second wealthiest man on the planet, with a net worth of around $180 billion.
Looking at the success of today, you would never guess that the company was started by a man who was homeless during his teenage years, had no education, and slept in a forest.
Louis Vuitton is a true rags to riches story, but the company would also be subject of a hostile takeover, countless lawsuits, and a host of other controversies.
This is the insane story of Louis Vuitton, and how a tiny family business evolved into one of the most powerful brands in the world.
Louis Vuitton was born in 1821 and grew up working on his family farm in France in a small village called Anki in the middle of nowhere.
They had no electricity and no running water.
Louis' father Xavier was a miller and farmer, whilst his mother Corinne made hats to help make some extra cash.
There are no records showing that Louis ever received an education.
The nearest school was in a village six miles away, and it's believed he worked full-time on the family farm without learning how to read or write.
Louis would have been working in the fields every day from dusk till dawn, just to make enough food to help feed his family.
Needless to say, the Vautons were struggling financially, and young Louis was born into a situation that should have doomed him from ever having a bright future.
And then, things got much worse.
Louis' mother died when he was just 10 years old, and his father quickly remarried another woman.
But Louis' new stepmother was incredibly controlling and manipulative towards him, and he constantly got into fights with her.
And so, when he was just 13 years old, he ran away from home with plans to go to Paris.
He slipped out in the middle of the night without even saying goodbye.
There was just one problem, Paris was 225 miles away, and Louis had no money or food, so he was forced to walk along dirt roads.
Most nights, he slept in the woods with an empty stomach and just a cloak to keep him warm.
Every time he ran into a new village, he would do odd jobs in exchange for food or coins.
However, there was never enough money left over for housing, so he continued to sleep in the woods, or wherever he could find shelter for the night.
Through these various odd jobs, Louis was able to pick up skills from craftsmen, and he learned how to work with metal, stone, fabric and wood.
This collection of various skills would later transform his life.
But at this rate, travel was incredibly slow.
It took him 3 years to reach Paris.
Not long after he arrived in Paris, Louis was able to work as an apprentice box maker and packer.
Box makers would make custom sized boxes for clients, as well as pack and unpack them whenever a client was about to go on a trip.

This job allowed him to meet many people from the upper class who were looking for custom made luggage for their travels, and Louis worked here for several years learning the craft and working as hard as he could.
In fact, in 1851, the Empress of France ended up being a customer and took notice of his fine craftsmanship.
She appointed him as her personal box maker and packer.
For most box makers, this would be the highest honour anyone could ever achieve in their career.
Louis had gone from a homeless teenager with nothing to his name to now working a prestigious job amongst royalty.
That was a massive achievement on its own.
But Louis Vuitton had an even bigger vision for his future.
After getting married when he was 33, Louis used his savings to start his own business, and opened up his own box making workshop in Paris to begin selling his own products.
You see Louis had noticed a major flaw in the luggage of the day.
All of the boxes were made of leather and had rounded dome shaped tops, so that rain would roll off the top of the luggage.
luggage.
The major issue was that it was impossible to stack them, so packers had to carry the boxes one by one.
Louis began experimenting with different materials to use instead, and found that canvas was lighter, durable and more water resistant, which meant the trunks could have flat tops instead.
This made everything more efficient, as it was now possible to stack them up in a pile and pack multiple trunks at the same time, and they were also more compact.
Louis's new suitcase design brought on the dawn of modern day luggage.
At this point Louis had already built up his professional reputation as well as connections to the upper class, so once he launched his new line of luggage it was immediately a huge success.
He even created a Louis Vuitton catalogue so that customers could look at products that he had available and have them made before sending it to their homes.

Within two years of creating his new suitcases, they were considered an elegant and must have accessory amongst the wealthy, as it became a status symbol, and the brand had become so popular that he was receiving orders from around the world.
He even began receiving orders from royals as far away as Egypt.
In 1859, Louis made enough profit to hire a team of craftsmen to help fulfil his orders.
He opened a new workshop outside of Paris, where he hired 20 employees.
Around that time, more and more people were beginning to travel by train and boat.
So the number of his potential customers increased exponentially.
Traveling was no longer a hobby exclusive to the rich.
People from all walks of life were now in need of high quality luggage.
It would seem as though Louis had made it, and would go on to succeed for the rest of his life.
Unfortunately, that was not the case.
France was heading to war, and tragedy was about to strike once again for Louis Vuitton.
So if you want a comfortable, stylish sneaker you can wear in all seasons, In 1870, when Louis was 49 years old, the Franco-Prussian War broke out.
Louis had to flee his home and live in a cramped shelter with thousands of others.
Food supplies were extremely low, and he feared for his life.
When Louis could finally return to his shop in 1871, everything was destroyed.
Windows were smashed, equipment was stolen, and he had lost everything he'd worked so hard for.
But instead of giving up, he decided to use his savings to rebuild the business, and vowed that it would be even better than it was before.
With so many people displaced from the war, there were far more empty shops available for rent throughout the city.
So Louis Vuitton took advantage of this by opening his new shop in a much more wealthy, aristocratic location in Paris.
It was perfect, because it was right next to the railway station and the Grand Hotel, so travellers who needed new luggage didn't need to go far to find the Louis Vuitton store.
By 1872 he came out with a brand new design, luggage made out of a beige canvas with stripes.
This became incredibly popular, and people loved showing off the modern style.
Many other brands tried to copy his style, but his bags were such ridiculously high quality that customers still preferred a true Louis Vuitton bag.
For the next 20 years, Louis continued to work at his new shop in Paris, until his death when he was 70 years old.
But his legacy was able to live on through his son George, who took over the family business.
George sought out to expand the brand globally, such as opening a popular store in London.
At this point, Louis Vuitton luggage was so popular that many other box makers were beginning to make counterfeits.
So in 1896, George Vuitton brought out the now iconic LV monogram to make it harder to copy.
The LV were his father's initials, in honour of the man who started the brand.
But he also came up with the idea of adding a revolutionary new lock on the trunks that would make it impossible for thieves to pick them.
By the year 1900, the company had 100 employees and it continued to grow year after year.
All of the employees were trained for a very long time in order to become expert box makers.
Even to this day, Louis Vuitton employees train for 18 months to 2 years before they're trusted to make one of the products on their own.
The company also began to expand into a whole new line of products because of another fashion icon, Coco Chanel.
In 1925 she commissioned a small dome shaped handbag.
At first this was a design that she personally came up with, and it was just for her.
However it would go on to be mass produced, and it was given the name Alma.
This was massively successful.
So Louis Vuitton decided to make more small leather bags like the Keepall, Speedy and No.
Before Louis Vuitton, handbags were often seen as quite inelegant and bulky, but the company played a big role in them being seen as much more fashionable.
George Vuitton died in 1936, and the company was then passed over to his son Gaston Louis.
However Gaston took over the company at a very difficult time, because in just a few years France was once again heading to war.
During World War II, contracts were cancelled and Gaston was forced to shut down the Louis Vuitton factory.
Paris was under siege again.
The only way Gaston Vuitton could save the business was to collaborate with Nazi Germany.
An author named Stephanie Bonvici wrote a book called Louis Vuitton, A French Saga.
During her research at the company archives, she asked if she could see records from World War II.
Almost immediately, the representatives from the company tried to avoid showing her the information.
They claimed that all of the documents from 1930 to 1945 were destroyed in a fire.

But after doing a lot of digging into other historic documents, Stephanie discovered that Louis Vuitton was able to open a glamorous ground floor shopfront in the Hotel de Parc throughout the Nazi regime, as they collaborated with them.
Meanwhile, several other brands were forced to shut down because they refused to cooperate with the Nazis.
Clearly, the company was ashamed of this part of their history.
But they would argue Gaston did what he needed to do in order for the company to survive.
Other fashion designers like Coco Chanel also collaborated with the Nazis in order to make sure her business in Paris was not destroyed.
If it were not for their choice to work with the enemy, their brands likely would no longer be around today.
When Gaston passed away in 1970, his son-in-law Henry Rackamere took over managing the Louis Vuitton brand.
So we're now onto the 4th generation.
But unlike his ancestors, Henry already had a lot of business experience from a company he'd run before, so when he took over Louis Vuitton, he was able to elevate the brand to a whole new level.
Henry began making major changes to the Louis Vuitton brand in order to grow it from a family-owned company to the massive corporation that it is today.
He switched Louis Vuitton's business model from wholesale to retail.
By 1978, he'd expanded Louis Vuitton into many other countries including Japan, and over the course of 6 years, and accounting for modern inflation, sales went from $20 million to $260 million.
And so in 1984, Henry decided to take the company public, and Louis Vuitton sold out the 1 million shares valued at $63.63 each.
Henry took this momentum and influx of cash and began opening more stores all across the globe.
By 1987, Louis Vuitton reached $1 billion in sales.
It was far beyond what young Louis could have ever dreamed of when he first opened his first store in Paris.
Henry also decided that the company should combine with Moet Hennessy, a luxury drinks company which produced champagne and cognac, and together they formed their new luxury conglomerate called LVMH.
In theory, by joining together, it would allow them to pool resources and expand even faster.

Unfortunately, after the merger, Henry didn't end up getting along well with the president of Moet Hennessy, so Henry asked a successful property developer he knew, named Bernard Arnault, to help him manage the situation.
Unfortunately, inviting him in as an investor would backfire in a huge way.
Bernard secretly bought 43% of the shares of Louis Vuitton, and got support from the Moet and Hennessy families to gain more power in LVMH.
Henry felt he'd been betrayed by the man he'd brought in to help him, and so took Bernard to court, demanding that he should no longer have the majority stake in Louis Vuitton.
But the courts ultimately sided with Bernard.
Henry was so angry about being backstabbed by his friend, that he decided to quit working for Louis Vuitton completely.
Now, for the first time in nearly 100 years, no one from the Vuitton family was involved with the brand.
After all of this drama of Bernard's hostile takeover, sales of Louis Vuitton began to crash.
Journalists were no longer covering the brand, and for a while it looked as though the company might fail.
However, Bernard knew how to turn the fortune of the company around.
Louis Vuitton was able to make a comeback when it began to collaborate with several fashion designers during its 100th anniversary collection.
Big names like Vivian Westwood and Isaac Misra all created their own take on the iconic LV Monogram logo.
They created products that customers had never seen before, and people were once again trying to get their hands on a Louis Vuitton bag.
Ultimately, Bernard's investment in Louis Vuitton paid off in a massive way.
He is now the CEO of LVMH, and in 2021, Forbes officially dubbed him the richest man in the world with a net worth of over $180 billion.
dollars.
Now of course as stock prices move, these rich list rankings change, but he's almost always in the top 5 richest people in the world.
However, out of the wealthiest people like Bezos, Musk, Gates, Buffett, Bernard Arnault is definitely the least known as he prefers to stay out of the spotlight.

What we do know is he has such a ruthless reputation in business, he is known as the wolf in cashmere, which is why today LVMH has over 70 different brands it owns through all of the acquisitions and mergers Bernard has pulled off.
This one company owns so many of the most luxurious brands in the world, and yet it all started with a broke homeless teenager.
In the modern world Louis Vuitton continued to expand its brand with new colourful styles that resonated with a younger audience.
In 1997 Marc Jacobs became the creative director.
He designed the first ready to wear line and also created the popular monogram vernice line of handbags.
Marc Jacobs also expanded LV into watches, jewellery and sunglasses, although he eventually would move on from Louis Vuitton and come up with his own line of clothing and accessories.
Of course, the company is not without its issues.
Louis Vuitton has an entire team of lawyers searching for copyright infringement, and they don't hesitate to sue someone if they believe that they're copying the brand logo.
They've even sued Google for search results and advertisements, leading people to fake bags.
Google won the case though, arguing they can't control what their users put on the internet.
Louis Vuitton has also gone on to collaborate with brands like Supreme, which expanded their demographic like never before.
Believe it or not though, Louis Vuitton actually sued Supreme as well for copying their logo, until they realised how profitable a collaboration would be.
Now, Louis Vuitton's Supreme items resell for a small fortune.
For example, the leather trunk is on sale for $125,000.
Well, even an LV Supreme hoodie is over $5,000.
Of course, the counterfeit problem Louis Vuitton had since the early days of the business is still an issue for the brand today.
They estimate that every year they lose hundreds of millions of dollars to counterfeit versions of their products.
However, even after being in business for 168 years, they don't seem to be slowing down anytime soon.
Louis Vuitton continues to be a brand that many people aspire to wear, and it's a staple among the rich and famous.
Currently, they are the number one fashion brand in the entire world, valued at $39 billion.
With more than 400 stores, you can find a Louis Vuitton in nearly every major city around the globe.

title: Why Red Bull Isn't A Drink Company
note: Origin of the drink, a partnership, then an explainer of the marketing machine, followed by controversies and lessons.
sections: Chaleo and Krating Daeng in Thailand
Founding Red Bull and launch prep
US debut and brand as story
lines: October 14th 2012.
Millions of viewers watch as skydiver Felix Baumgartner ascends to the edge of space, takes a small step and then free falls about 120,000 feet down to earth.
During his descent, he not only broke the sound barrier, but a handful of world records as well.
However, this spectacle was not from NASA or SpaceX.
When you look a little closer, you see the unmistakable symbol of Red Bull.
Of course, this is just one of countless examples of Red Bull's extreme and unorthodox marketing strategies.
They're responsible for 10-story motorcycle jumps, snowboarding down an active volcano, not to mention owning multiple racing, football and esports teams.
So, how did this simple energy drink?
which started out as an obscure medicinal syrup, become not only one of the biggest disruptors in the beverage industry, but also one of the best marketed products ever.

By the end of 2022, the global energy drink industry will be worth around $90 billion, and sitting on top of the caffeinated throne is Red Bull, who in 2021 alone sold more than 9.8 billion cans across 172 countries, more than one can for every person on the planet.
And yet, despite this, Red Bull began from the most unlikely and humble of beginnings.
Chaelio Uvidya was born in rural Thailand, and his parents were duck farmers who also sold fruit.
They had very little money, and couldn't afford to give their children a formal education.
Thus, Chaelio grew up working on a farm with very little prospects.

However, when his parents sent him off to Bangkok to go and work with his brother as a pharmaceutical sales rep, he worked extremely hard, and saved up enough money that in 1956, he was able to open his own small business, which he called TC Pharmaceutical Industries.
Initially, the business was designed purely to sell medicines, such as antibiotics that he imported.
However, around this time, pharmaceutical companies in Japan had started creating herbal syrups labelled energising tonics.
They were a big hit, and soon started getting imported to Thailand as well.
After nearly 10 years of running TC Pharmaceutical Industries, Chaleo decided he wanted to create his own version of these energy tonics.
However, Chaleo saw that the current products on the market were quite expensive and targeted more towards wealthier consumers.
Given that he came from poverty himself, he knew that it was actually the blue collar working man who needed the energy much more.
Construction workers, farmers, people doing lots of physical labour which required constant attention and energy.
So after analysing the formulas of other drinks on the market, Chaleo created his own similar elixir containing caffeine, B vitamins, and a chemical called taurine.
But what truly set Chaleo's concoction apart from the competition was the inclusion of large amounts of sugar, giving the syrup a more appealing flavour, and even more of an energy boost.
He named the beverage Kratting Deng.

In Thai, Deng means red, which for him symbolised perseverance, but Kratting doesn't actually mean ball, it means gore, which is a relative of the water buffalo, and the largest species of wild cattle in the world.
The reason for the choice is that Chaleo wanted the brand rooted in imagery of strength and power.
However, his drink was hardly an overnight success.
At the time, products from countries like Japan and South Korea dominated the market.
But Chaleo's decision to focus more on provincial and rural parts of Thailand, unlike his competitors who focused on big cities like Bangkok, proved to be a wise choice.
To get things started, Chaleo gave some free samples to truck drivers who were working long hours and needed help staying alert, and he pitched it as a stimulant to improve energy and concentration.
It then steadily grew via word of mouth and began to grow in popularity amongst Thailand's working class.
Using the money from initial sales, Che Lio began sponsoring Mai Tai matches, which was the most popular martial art in Thailand, and a big part of Thai culture.
This not only helped his drink get recognition, but created an association with high energy and power.

This was a great strategy, because most of the other energy drinks at the time were pretty generic, whereas right from the start Che Lio focused on building a brand, and his drink almost became a symbol of perseverance amongst the working class.
By 1980, his product had become a big success all over Thailand.
However, it was an unlikely encounter with an Austrian businessman selling toothpaste that would soon make this drink a multi-billion dollar global empire.
Whilst it was Chaelio who first created the drink that would later become known as Red Bull, it was a man named Dietrich Mateschitz who helped the business become what it is today.
Dietrich had studied world trade at the University of Commerce in Vienna, although between partying, travelling and chasing girls, it took him 10 years to graduate.

However, he was always known for his wild imaginative ideas, and after graduating had worked his way up to become international marketing director of a German company called Blendax, who manufactured products like skin creams, shampoo and toothpaste.
As part of his job, Dietrich had to travel all over the world.
world.
This meant many long days and nights of airports and flights.

On one particularly exhausting trip from Europe to Thailand, where he was meant to be attending an important meeting, he felt so tired that he went into a local store and asked if there was anything that could help him.
It was here that he discovered Chaelio's energy drink, Kratting Deng.
Dietrich tried it, and in just a few minutes he not only felt more energised, he no longer had his jet lag.
He became an avid drinker of the product, but at this time it was only available in Thailand.
Shortly after this, Dietrich read a newspaper that the highest taxpayer in Japan was another one of these energy drinks.
This confirmed to him just how popular these products were in Asia, and yet there was nothing really like it in the West.
Now, to be honest, Dietrich had been getting kinda bored of his job at Blendax, and so he decided to make a very bold move.
He quit his well-paying job, and tracked down Chaleo, saying he wanted to go into business with him.
Dietrich's plan was to take Chaleo's energy drink international, and introduce it to European consumers.
After a little persuading, the two men went into business together, each putting in $500,000 of their savings.
They agreed Dietrich would run the operational side, whilst Cheleo would continue to focus on the product side.
They both got 49% of the company, with the remaining 2% going to Cheleo's son.
Dietrich's first big decision was they should form a new separate company for this called Red Bull, which would be simpler and more memorable than the literal translation of Red Gore.
And thus in 1984, Red Bull officially was founded in Dietrich's home country of Austria.
However, before launching, they did some customer research to test how European audiences responded to the product, and the feedback was awful.

Trial groups said the drink tasted disgusting, and market research suggested the drink was too unhealthy and not appealing at all, but the two Red Bull founders so strongly believed in the idea that they pushed on anyway.
They made some important changes using the feedback though, like carbonating the drink and switching to a slimmer, sleek silver can which looked more premium and distinguished it from competitors.
Dietrich also said that in order to feel like a premium product, they had to have a premium price, and so they charged nearly double what consumers were used to paying for other carbonated drinks.
Pricing this high seemed like a very risky move, but would later be crucial to the company's success.
They also decided on the now famous slogan, Red Bull gives you wings, to represent a product that provides energy, focus and potential.
This would later cause controversy though.
But for now in 1987, Red Bull was finally ready to be released in the West.
On April 1st, 1987, Red Bull launched in Austria, and to create the premium feel Dietrich wanted, the beverage was initially offered at trendy Austrian ski resorts.
To begin with, Red Bull had a very small team of just a single secretary and a six person sales force.
And since they had an extremely small marketing budget, Dietrich knew he couldn't afford expensive TV ads or elaborate campaigns like other drinks companies.
Instead, he initially relied on more creative, lower cost marketing strategies to spread the word about Red Bull.
Firstly, they reached out to popular, charismatic and influential college students.
They would then give them cases of Red Bull for free and have them drive around campus in mini coopers decorated with enormous Red Bull cans on top.
They also gave these students money to throw parties where Red Bull was given out.
The idea was that these popular students would shape the buying habits of their friends and fellow students.
In fact, they even started hiring attractive women to be Red Bull girls and just hand out free drinks on university campuses.

Meanwhile, Red Bull salespeople, called mesquiteers, offered free coolers to bars, inspiring bartenders to feature the beverage in new cocktails, which helped Red Bull become known as a mixer with alcoholic drinks.
Red Bull even began leaving empty cans in bars and nightclubs so that people would constantly see the logo and be curious to try the drink themselves.
All these tactics proved successful, and Red Bull sold over 1 million cans in the first year.
However, financially, they actually made a loss that year, since they'd given away so many free products as part of their marketing schemes.
But Dietrich knew that investing in their brand, especially in the early stages, would pay dividends later.
And he was right.
By the second year, sales doubled to 2 million cans, and again to 4 million cans by the third year.
Red Bull spread across Europe and at one point got so popular in Germany that they couldn't produce enough cans to keep up with the demand.

Of course, despite the growth, competing in mainstream advertising like TV ads was still a very expensive option, but Dietrich had always loved extreme sports, and realised that very few big companies seemed to be sponsoring these events, like for example cliff diving.
Sponsoring extreme sports helped sell Red Bull as more than just an energy drink, but a lifestyle.
Red Bull became associated with daredevils and high adrenaline activities.
By 1997, Red Bull was ready for its US debut.
Although by that point, the energy drink market had become a $1.7 billion business, and thus a lot more competition had entered the market.
And unlike other beverage rivals, such as Coca-Cola, Red Bull had no secret, patented formula.
All the ingredients are clearly labelled on the can.
And initially, Red Bull literally just offered one flavour, which typically performed poorly in taste tests.
And yet, despite all this, Red Bull sales continued to rise.

In an interview, Dietrich was asked why he didn't try to make a better tasting product, to which he replied that Red Bull was never about the product itself, but building a brand around an experience.
You see, at its core, Red Bull never set out to be a beverage company, it was a storytelling company.
The goal was to bring customers into the evolving myth, instead of trying to cram a product into their lives.
To achieve this, the company had taken great efforts to attach itself to a growing collection of events and spectacles that entice customers to the brand.

Red Bull spends far more than most companies on marketing, but instead of merely running ads on why you should buy the drink or sponsoring a single event, Red Bull will purchase entire sports teams, construct in-house media companies and host world class events.
It all began with Austrian Formula 1 legend Gerhard Berger, who became Red Bull's first sponsored athlete in 1989.

But today, the company sponsors over 500 athletes, daredevils and adventurers, spanning the entire field of professional and amateur sports, from football to ice hockey to Formula 1 and now even esports.

Interestingly, this has actually opened up other revenue streams for the company, for example they make money from Formula 1 prizes and sponsorships, giving them yet more money to reinvest in marketing.

But this long term approach is extremely effective, because for example, by owning a team like the New York Red Bulls, every time the media or fans are discussing the team, it's naturally bringing Red Bull into conversation and people's subconscious.
The company has even invented its own sporting events, The Flugtag, created in 2000, is the German word for flying day.
During this event Red Bull created, hundreds of teams worldwide compete in homemade flying machines to see how far their wild creations can fly.
And if you're wondering, the current record stands at 258 feet.
By creating events in which its product can be served and its brand narrative can unfold, Red Bull has again successfully turned expenses into a successful revenue stream all on its own.
Outside of the world of sports, Red Bull also sponsors art and music events, such as Lollapalooza and Austin City Limits.
And of course by 2012, the company was sending daredevils to the edge of space to jump out on freefall at over 800mph.
And despite taking years to plan and tens of millions of dollars, it seems like this was worth it.
The YouTube video of this set a world record for most concurrent livestreams and has gone on to reach well over 120 million views.
And right after this, the company saw global sales rise by 13%.
When Red Bull create these memorable events or set world records, they're often talked about or watched long after they happen, providing a great steady long term return on their investment.
But here's the most interesting and unique part of Red Bull's strategy.
During all of these events and spectacles the company puts on, they hardly ever refer to their drink.

For example, with Felix Baumgartner's record breaking freefall, most companies would probably have made sure that when he landed he was seen drinking a can of Red Bull, but there was no mention of the drink.
And that's because Red Bull's advertising so often doesn't feel like advertising.
Red Bull aim for brand recognition rather than actively selling their products.
They tried to make something genuinely exciting for their audience to simply associate their brand with incredible things.
And in a world where we are inundated with ads in our face and sales pitches, this more subtle approach is effective, as then it doesn't cheapen the spectacle.
It doesn't feel like we're watching an ad, it feels like we're just watching something cool from a company who happens to also sell energy drinks.
The truth is Red Bull isn't really a drinks company, it's a marketing company.
And as a result, they've been able to position Red Bull as more of a premium lifestyle product, which is ironic because it's the total opposite of how it began in Thailand for blue collar workers.
Red Bull started out as the cheapest energy drink, now it's one of the most expensive.
The recipe hasn't really changed, that's just the power of great marketing and branding.
As a result, in some countries today, Red Bull has more than 80% market share of energy drinks, and since 1987, over 100 billion cans have been sold worldwide.
However, you don't become the number one energy drink without a little controversy.
Red Bull has been banned in numerous countries over the years, most famously in France.
When a teenager died after drinking multiple cans of Red Bull during a basketball match, there was understandably a lot of panic.

Now, there was no evidence found that Red Bull caused the death, but it still prompted accusations that the drink's caffeine content was excessive and that some of Red Bull's other ingredients might not be as safe as they made out.
However, by 2008, the full version of Red Bull was for sale in France again, since Red Bull successfully argued there wasn't sufficient evidence that any of the ingredients were harmful.
I mean, it wasn't exactly healthy, but not unhealthy enough to be banned.
Then in Germany in 2009, Red Bull Cola was found to contain trace amounts of cocaine, causing some German states to pull the drink as well.
But once again, after further research it was found to be such a negligible amount that you'd have to drink almost impossible amounts to actually feel anything.
So the drink was reinstated there too.
In 2013, Red Bull came under fire again when it was sued for false advertising over its slogan, Red Bull Gives You Wings.
Now to be fair to Red Bull here, surely nobody actually expected to grow literal wings and fly, so this lawsuit seemed like a frivolous cash grab.
But they managed to argue that since Red Bull didn't give any functional athletic improvement, it was false advertising, and Red Bull ended up paying $13 million to settle the lawsuit.
Now, so far, all of these issues seem kind of harsh against Red Bull, but actually, the real controversy about Red Bull is the one that most people in the West don't even seem to know about.
You see, in 2012, the heir to Red Bull's fortune, Chilio's grandson, was accused of running over a policeman and killing him while speeding in his Ferrari.
It's then reported he didn't attend court and instead fled the country.

Despite there being seemingly overwhelming informing evidence against them, the case has not been pursued, and in Thailand it's seen as an egregious example of how the ultra-wealthy and powerful are above the law and can get away with anything.
This prompted headlines like Red Bull Air shows how to get away with killing a cop in Thailand, with some even starting a campaign to boycott Red Bull.

Now to be fair, it's not like the air to Red Bull's fortune was actually involved in running the company, but it's certainly a stain on the perfect image that Red Bull spend so much money to maintain.
However, Red Bull's original creator Che Leo would not be around to see that, as he died just a few months before the incident in March 2012, aged 88.
When he passed away, he was Thailand's third richest person with an estimated $5 billion fortune.
And in fact, to this day, his co-founder Dietrich is the richest person in Austria.
That's because Red Bull is still a private company.
The founders never had to sell loads of their equity, as they had such great profit margins and could keep reinvesting back into the business using the profits they made.
So they both became obscenely wealthy.
And actually, I think there's several lessons all of us should be learning from Red Bull.
Firstly, Red Bull is proof that sometimes you don't need to invent something totally new.
You can bring an existing product to a new market or audience, and have massive success by just putting your own spin on it.

Secondly, it's clearly a very effective strategy to find a product that's cheap to manufacture, and then invest heavily in marketing to create a more premium feel and brand image for the product so you can charge higher prices.
That'll give you high profit margins, giving you huge amounts of money to invest in even more marketing, and thus create a virtuous cycle of growth.
For context, some sources have estimated Red Bull costs about 9 cents per can to make, yet they sell them for $1.79 or more.
And finally, Red Bull is a reminder that the best marketing is not just running ads the exact same way everyone else does, it's actually doing something creative and original.
Because the ultimate lesson from Red Bull is to not just sell a product, but sell a feeling.
Sell an image.

title: The Poor Boy Who Created Honda
note: Cradle-to-grave biography with repeated setback-and-adapt cycles; sponsor break placed at the cliffhanger before the car chapter.
lines: For many people in Japan, it was an ordinary day on November 17th 1906.
However, it was also the birth of Soichiro Honda, who would go on to change the world in more ways than one.
Honda's father was a blacksmith who had a bicycle repair shop, whilst his mother worked as a weaver.
Their family was very poor and of Honda's 8 siblings, 5 of them died during childhood due to poor health.

However, as Honda grew up, he became very interested in tools and machines, and was especially keen on learning how vehicles worked after he saw his first car, a Ford Model T, whilst he was just a toddler.
He chased after it, mesmerised by its design.
That memory and the smell of the oil would stay with him forever.
Now around this time, bicycles were becoming very popular all over Japan, and customers began to line up in front of his father's repair shop.
Honda spent a lot of time watching his dad work, and then practicing repairs himself.
Honda even learned how to make his own toys from whatever materials he saw lying around.
Within a few years, Honda was regularly helping his dad out in the repair shop.
However, when it came to academic learning, Honda did terribly in school.
He just wasn't interested in what they were teaching, and longed to be back in his father's workshop instead.
Since he lacked interest in school, his grades suffered.
The class were given reports with their grades on which they were meant to take to their parents, who would then stamp a family seal on it to show they'd seen the report card.

However, Honda didn't want his parents to see he was failing and disappoint them, so he decided to create a family seal using a scrap rubber bicycle pedal cover so that his teacher would think his parents had stamped it.
And it it worked.

In fact, it worked so well that other kids in his class who were afraid of showing their low grades to their parents, came to him asking if he could create family seals for them as well, so they didn't have to show their parents their report card.
Eventually though, Honda got caught, and his dad wasn't mad he'd done it, his dad was mad his work had been sloppy enough to get found out.
Despite not getting much of a formal education, Honda was quickly developing his skills in his father's workshop, and had a genuine fascination with machinery and engineering.
Then in 1917, when Honda was 11 years old, he heard that a pilot named Art Smith was going to demonstrate the aerobatic capabilities of the biplane.
So he decided to borrow some money from the petty cash box, took one of the bicycles in his father's shop and rode for 20km to the military's airfield to watch the show.
Except when he got there, he realised he didn't actually have enough money for the admission fee, so he decided to climb up a tree to watch the demonstration.
Honda found it incredible, and this only increased his love for machinery and invention.
But when he returned home, his father had discovered what had happened.

Luckily, instead of being angry, Honda's father was far more impressed at his son's determination and initiative, and perhaps deep down he was proud his son had the same appreciation for engineering that he did.
So he let the incident pass.
In 1922 after finishing school, Honda spotted an advertisement in a newspaper for a car servicing company named Art Shokai.
The ad said, assistant wanted for auto repair shop in Tokyo.
He figured that if the company could afford to be running ads like this, maybe they'd have spaces available for apprenticeships for young men like him wanting to get into the trade.
So at the age of just 15, he decided to leave home in search of a job, and headed to Tokyo.
Going from his small village to the bustling streets of Tokyo was an intense experience, but his hunch had been right, and he was able to get an apprenticeship working at Art Shokai Garage.
Unfortunately, on his first day he was given the job of cleaning up, scrubbing the dirty floors, and preparing meals for the owners.
In fact, he would often end up babysitting the owners child, so not exactly what he'd had in mind.
Plus apprenticeships at the time weren't paid, so he was merely given a small space to rest and a bit of food to eat.
But soon after joining, an earthquake hit Tokyo, which caused many of the mechanics to have to leave work for a while to repair their homes.
The auto repair shop was now understaffed, and Honda finally got his chance, as he was asked to fill in as a mechanic.
By working extremely hard, this role was soon made permanent.
Honda was eager to learn and spent his days repairing cars and motorcycles, which at the time were limited to only the upper class.
It was here that Honda encountered a very wide range of vehicles from all different manufacturers, which sharpened his knowledge even more.
Honda would always take a lot of care in examining each vehicle assigned to him for repair, and on his work breaks, he'd read whatever car-related magazines he could get his hands on.
It wasn't long before Honda was not just repairing vehicles, but designing spare parts as well.

Given that Honda was doing a lot of great work for this company, one of the owners, named Yuzo, took it upon himself to educate Honda about the business side of the trade, as well as the technical side.
Yuzo was the ideal mentor for Honda, and it was him who introduced Honda to the world of motorsports.
You see, in 1923, Yuzo had decided to begin manufacturing his own race car, and he asked Honda to help him out with building it.
Their second design, which they named the Curtis, ended up winning the 1924 Japanese Motor Car Championship.

Honda was on board as the accompanying engineer, and this victory at a young age, both winning the race and the thrill of helping to build something like this, was a feeling he'd never forget, and a feeling he'd continue to chase.
When he turned 20, Honda was called up to fulfil his obligations in military service.
However, during the medical examination, it was found out he was colourblind, and he was excused from duty.

Shortly after this in 1928, his mentor, the owner of Archokai, presented him with an opportunity, saying that he wanted Honda to set up his own branch of Archokai in Hamamatsu, a Japanese city very close to the village where Honda was born.
Given Honda was still in his early 20s, it was a lot of responsibility to run his own auto repair shop.
But he clearly impressed his managers, and so Honda gladly accepted.

Honda's branch grew slowly at first, it was just him running it all by himself initially, and when people brought their cars in for repairs, some were put off by how young he seemed, assuming that he was inexperienced.
But he eventually managed to build up a good reputation in the area, and by the mid-1930s, he'd managed to hire a full team to help.
At last, Honda was making good money for himself.
He'd worked his way up from an unpaid apprentice looking after his boss's baby, to running his own successful auto repair shop.
And as a rich young man, Honda was never shy about having a good time.
There are many reports of him enjoying himself in the company of lots of geishas, stories of him throwing parties, and even dancing nude at his wedding.
Honda worked hard, but he partied even harder.
However, sometimes his nights of drinking did not end so well.
There was one incident whilst drunk, where he accidentally knocked Geisha out of a window from the second floor.

Fortunately, she survived by landing on some wires, although they reportedly had to cut the electrical wires to save the woman, which resulted in the entire town experiencing an electrical power outage.

Honda also continued to enjoy racing, but that too would nearly end in a fatal disaster, when in 1936 Honda was involved in a serious car crash during the Japanese high-speed rally that forced him to quit racing completely.
He spent three months in hospital, and had a permanent scar for the rest of his life.
The doctors commented that he was lucky to get out alive at all.
The incident was a wake up call for Honda.
Suddenly having an influx of wealth had led him to a bit of a playboy, daredevil lifestyle, but several close encounters had made him re-evaluate what he really wanted.
He realised that even though his auto repair shop was doing well, he was dissatisfied with car repair.
It was time for a new and bigger challenge.
Honda saw a lot of potential in manufacturing, and asked Art Shokai if he could turn his auto repair shop he was running for them into a separate company where he would produce piston rings.
Unfortunately, Art Shokai did not like this idea at all.

The business was doing well and making a lot of money, they had no interest in stopping that and entering a whole new field, especially since producing their own car parts rather than repairing them, seemed like a lot more risk and cost.
However, Honda was determined to pursue his new vision, so he and a friend decided to go into business together, setting up their own separate business called Tokai Seiko Heavy Industry.
At first Honda would still spend his days working at his repair shop and then spend his nights working on this new car part manufacturing company he'd started, trying to create piston rings.
It was exhausting trying to do both though, and he didn't get much sleep.
He also took evening classes to improve his understanding of metals and alloys, and for two years he worked tirelessly, until he reached a revolutionary piston design breakthrough in 1939.
At this point, he turned over his duties at Art Shokai to his trainees, and began to fully focus on this new manufacturing company.
They began piston production, and for the first time in a while, Honda felt truly excited by his work again.
But that excitement was short lived, as they were soon bombarded with manufacturing challenges.
For example, they received an order from Toyota, but of the thousands of pistons they ordered from Honda's company, only 3 passed Toyota's high quality standards.
It was a big setback.
But Honda decided he'd go visit universities and factories all over Japan to further understand the manufacturing process and develop his skills further.
Eventually, he obtained enough knowledge and skill that he was able to produce piston rings that passed Toyota's quality standards.
And better yet, Honda figured out a way to mass produce them using an automated process which meant even unskilled labourers could produce them.
This meant he was able to produce them in bulk at a relatively low cost.
Orders rapidly increased, and since Honda couldn't keep up with demand from his workshop, he opened a factory to mass produce the piston rings.
Unfortunately, just as Honda's manufacturing business was really taking off, Japan was gearing up for war.
When Japan entered World War 2 in 1941, many of Honda's male employees were called for military service, leaving Honda's plant with lots of vacant positions.
The war also meant that there were a lot of supply shortages, and Honda had difficulty sourcing materials.
When enemy planes dropped fuel cans out of the sky, Honda would tell his employees to look for the fallen cans as they could still be used for manufacturing.
That's how desperate for supplies he was.
In 1944, it was beginning to look like Japan would lose the war, and when a bomb was dropped on one of Honda's factories, it looked like he might lose his business.
In another cruel twist, just a year later, Honda's other factory would be destroyed in an earthquake.
It was soul-destroying that what he'd spent years building was quite literally turned to rubble.
The company had already been struggling immensely because of the war, but this was the final nail in the coffin for his company.
He was going out of business.
So Honda sold whatever was left of his manufacturing business to Toyota.
There was a massive fuel shortage after the war, and transportation at this time was limited mostly to bicycles.
People needed a way to get around easily and cheaply whilst being extremely fuel efficient.
So Honda had an idea.
He attached a small motor to his bike, which soon caught the attention of people all around the city.

Sensing this could be a good solution to his country's problems, Honda created the Honda Technical Research Institute in 1946 using the money he had left after selling his piston ring manufacturing business.
The sole purpose of this was to figure out the best way to make motorbikes.
Using some surplus military engines Honda had managed to obtain, he was able to successfully build working motorbikes that immediately became a hit in Japan.
Soon he was flooded with orders and ran out of used engines, so Honda developed his own engine.
However, to be able to mass produce enough motorbikes to fulfil the demand, Honda needed more money to invest in production.
And unfortunately, in the bleak economic conditions following the war, investment was not easily available.
But as always, Honda found a way.
He reportedly wrote letters to 18,000 bicycle shop owners across the country explaining his idea, and asking them to invest in his new motorbike design.
3,000 of those bicycle shop owners wrote back to say they'd invest in Honda's motorbikes.
So Honda was back in business.
Honda Motors Co was incorporated in 1948 to manufacture small capacity motorcycles with the goal of producing an affordable motorbike which would help Japanese people more easily get around.

Honda also teamed up with business partner Takeo Fujisawa who provided not only additional investment for the company but also was a great business operator and strategist, allowing Honda more time to devote to the product side of the business.
Honda's first fully fledged motorbike was the D-Type, which stood for Dream, although it was a bit too bulky and heavy.
But Honda soon found success with a new and improved model called the Super Cub, which was lighter, smaller and safer, and an immediate success.
Orders poured in from all over the country.
Honda then turned its focus to entering the US market.
But prior to the 1960s, the stereotypical image of the American motorcyclist was that of a rough, unruly, unsavoury character.
So to try and change this, Honda ran an extremely successful advertising campaign with the slogan, you meet the nicest people on a Honda.
This, mixed with the more lightweight design, encouraged families and younger people to disassociate the motorcycle from previous stereotypes, and thus reach a whole new market with their motorbikes.
As a result, nearly one out of every two motorbikes sold in the US in 1964 was a Honda motorcycle.
And pretty soon, small lightweight motorcycles were zipping all across American roads.
And by the end of the 1960s, Honda was the biggest motorcycle company in the world, producing about a million per month.
In fact, Honda is still the largest motorcycle producer to this day.
Not only was Honda a financial success, it was a racing success too.
In 1966, Honda Motors took home the Constructors' Championships in all 5 motorcycle classes in the Grand Prix, as the team with the most points at the end of the season.
By this point, Honda Bikes had won pretty much all of the major racing titles there was to win.
Honda Motorbikes were a huge success by all metrics.
But Soichiro Honda still had one dream left that he hadn't fulfilled.
It was finally time for his biggest and most ambitious project to date.

Ever since seeing his first car as a child, Honda had wanted to produce his own, and given his own humble beginnings, he especially liked the idea of making an affordable, quality car so almost everyone could experience having one.

However, almost everyone told Honda that now he'd found success with making motorbikes, he should stick to that, as there was so much more competition in the car market, especially in America where the big car brands were so dominant.
But Honda had always been a risk taker, and after feeling like he'd conquered two wheels, he was now ready to move on to four.
Honda Motorco's first Osmobile attempt was actually the T360 mini truck, which went on sale in 1963.
But it wasn't popular, and never sold very well.
But as always though, when Honda got a setback like this, it just meant he had to figure out a new approach.
Now in the early 70s there was a growing environmental movement, with more concern about air quality and pollution.
This resulted in US cities introducing the Clean Air Act, which forced stricter regulations on vehicles.
Immediately, all of the big car manufacturers!
The new rules were impossible, whereas Honda simply said, I'll find a way, and set about to build a new revolutionary engine that passed the new pollution tests.
