It was called the Compound Vortex Controlled Combustion Engine, and was not only more environmentally friendly but also allowed people to travel further using less fuel.
So whilst the established forces in the American car market were lobbying to scrap the regulations, Honda had been taking action and finding a solution.
Honda himself would later comment, when Congress passes new emission standards, we hire 50 more engineers, and GM hires 50 more lawyers.
By 1972, he'd come up with the Honda Civic, which would be the first car to use this new CVCC engine.
This energy efficient, compact and lightweight passenger car was the perfect answer to the oil crisis of 1973, where gas prices were so high.
The Honda Civic was light on fuel, low on emissions and reliable.
Essentially, it was the perfect car at the perfect time.
And the Honda Civic would soon become one of the most popular cars in the world.
When sales of the Honda Civic crossed 1 million, Honda Motors then introduced the Accord.
This was the more upscale model, intended to attract middle class drivers looking to mix great design with a practical price point.
Through word of mouth, Honda started to develop a reputation for reliability.
Sales were increasing, and Honda established itself as one of the leading car manufacturers.

When the Accord proved to be popular, Honda confidently entered the luxury car market as well by introducing the Acura brand to America in 1986, which also raked in large sales both in the US and Japan.
Honda now had multiple different offerings for different types of consumers, all of which were selling well.
Thus, by the end of the 1980s, Honda was the third largest car company on the planet.
After grappling with liver failure, Soichiro Honda succumbed to the disease and died in 1991.
Upon his death, he held an estimated net worth of $92 million.
In total, he'd registered over 150 different patents for different inventions.
He had three sons, but none of them inherited the company.
Honda and his business partner believed in meritocracy instead of nepotism, and that a business will survive when handled by highly skilled professionals rather than unskilled family members.
Despite the massive loss of its founder, Honda Motors went on to conquer the American market through comprehensive reorganizations, improved automobile designs, and innovative marketing efforts.
Of course, still to this day, Honda is one of the leading global car manufacturers, but has also gone on to expand into all kinds of new products, from jets to robots.
It's crazy really, as Honda's life started out so bleak, with just a simple curiosity and love for working with tools and machines.
But Honda knew what he wanted, and he committed to it.
He took action and adjusted his approaches when things didn't work out as he'd expected.
He understood that if you make a superior product, people will buy it.
And he worked tirelessly to make that happen.

title: How A Kid With $0 Created Nike
note: Long biography built on a chain of crises (scam fear, supplier betrayal, customs bill, labour scandal), each resolved by a bold decision; two Shopify reads and a subscribe ask interrupt.
sections: Break with Onitsuka, Nike name and swoosh
lines: Phil Knight suddenly woke up.
He'd just been having a nightmare where his life had no purpose.
Except, it wasn't just a dream, this was his reality.
Unsure what to do with his life, Phil went to the University of Oregon where he studied journalism and developed his interest in running.
It was here that he met with the track coach Bill Bowerman, a famous coach in America who'd trained Olympic athletes.
Phil trained under Bowerman as a middle distance runner and the two men struck up a great friendship.
They didn't know it at the time, but that friendship would later become the foundation of the biggest sports company in the world.
But, we'll get to that.
After graduating with a journalism degree in 1959, Phil was still very confused about what to do with his life.
Deep down, he'd wanted to become an athlete, but at 24 years old, he had to admit it.
The dream was dead.
Despite all the lessons and training at college, he just hadn't got to the level needed.
And now, he felt lost.
Phil even enlisted in the army and completed a year of service, thinking that might give him a sense of direction.
It didn't.
He was left frustrated and angry.
So, after the army, Phil enrolled in the Graduate School of Business at Stanford University, and it was here at Stanford that he finally found his calling.
Whilst working on an assignment to invent a new business, Phil had had an idea that would change his life forever.
On a piece of paper, he wrote, You see, Phil had noticed how two Japanese camera companies, Nikon and Canon, had replaced German cameras in the market, which used to be much more dominant.
and he wondered if the same thing could happen with running shoes.
Now at the time, two German companies, Adidas and Puma, were the leading running shoe brands in America and they had a very strong hold of the market.
But Phil had heard the Japanese were experimenting with some new shoe designs and he also knew that it would be cheaper to produce shoes in Japan as well.

So Phil got extremely invested in this assignment for his business class and genuinely started to believe there was a great business opportunity here to import Japanese shoes into the American market.
But when Phil presented this to the class, because nobody else seemed to see it that way.
He even told some of his friends about the idea, but none of them seemed to pay much attention either.
Of course, if Phil did want to actually pursue this idea himself, he knew how difficult it would be.
He didn't know anyone in Japan to reach out to, and he knew absolutely nothing about importing Japanese shoes, or even how to sell them in America for that matter.
So, could he really just do it?
After graduating from business school in 1962, Phil found himself back at home living with his parents.
That familiar feeling was back that his life was just passing him by, and he needed to do something meaningful.
One day, Phil finally decided he couldn't just keep waiting for some magic opportunity, and he had to go and create an opportunity for himself.
So Phil and one of his friends decided to take a long trip to go travelling around the world.

Phil had stayed obsessed with his idea of bringing Japanese shoes to the American market, and so he figured as part of the trip, he would visit Japan to see if he could make his crazy idea into a reality.
But first, they visited classic European cities, backpacked through Asia, and even stopped in Greece, where Phil saw the Temple of Athena Nike, dedicated to the Goddess of Victory.
Phil and his friend then went to Hawaii, and that's where things changed.
Phil and his friend surfed, relaxed on the beach, and loved the whole place so much, they ended up getting jobs in Honolulu, selling encyclopedias door to door.
simply so they could afford to stay in this Hawaiian paradise a little longer.
However, Phil was pretty shy and didn't do well at the sales job at all, and eventually he decided he'd done enough relaxing and it was time to leave.
His friend had met a girl and stayed behind though, so Phil said goodbye and continued his trip alone.
And Phil already knew exactly where he wanted to go next.
It was time to get serious about his dream.
It was time to go to Japan.
In 1962 in the city of Kobe, Phil came across one particular running shoe that caught his eye.
The brand was called Tiger, and the shoes were manufactured by a company called Onitsuka.
Not only did he like the design, the shoes ticked the two main criteria Phil needed, they were clearly high quality shoes and yet they were relatively cheap.
Phil liked the shoes so much that he cold called the owners of the shoe brand and managed to arrange a meeting.
Feeling both nervous and excited, Phil put on a suit and went to meet the manufacturers of the Japanese shoe he liked so much.
Before going, he bought a copy of How to Do Business with the Japanese, and memorised as much information as he could.
Despite Phil having zero expertise in the business, he introduced himself in the meeting as an American shoe distributor, who was going to help market their shoes in America.
It turns out that Onitsuka had been looking for a way to sell its shoes in America already, so they were actually very excited when Phil came to them with the same idea.
Perhaps that's why they were willing to overlook the fact that Phil looked like he was fresh out of university, which he quite literally was.

But despite being a recent graduate in his 20s with no actual experience of running a business, Phil had memorised lots of facts and statistics about the American shoe market from his assignment at university, and so he was basically able to recite parts of his presentation during the meeting, and so it looked like he completely knew what he was talking about.
The Japanese managers were impressed.
However, one of them asked Phil a very simple question, what's the name of the company you're from?
Phil suddenly felt his heart beating faster.
Of course the truth was, Phil didn't have a company name, because he didn't actually have a company yet, he just had this crazy idea to import Japanese shoes to America.
Phil's mind started racing.

For a split second he felt completely out of his depth and just wanted to be back home with his parents, and that's when his mind suddenly flashed to the blue ribbons from his childhood that he used to have hung up on his wall.
After a second pause, Phil replied, He just kinda blurted the name out of nowhere, since in truth he'd never expected to get this far.
But after inventing a company name on the spot, Phil could feel his confidence increasing.
He went on to explain the size of the American market, and how Onitsuka's tiger shoes were different to what they had in America, meaning there was a huge opportunity if Onitsuka and him teamed up.

The Japanese company was so keen, they basically began pitching Phil, and asked him if he would be their distribution partner in the US, to which Phil obviously agreed, and then he asked them to ship over some samples to his address in America.
It seemed like Phil's crazy idea was about to become a reality.
One month, two months, three months, four months, the time kept passing and no shoe samples arrived.
Phil couldn't understand it, he'd returned to America so excited and optimistic, because it seemed like his meeting with the Japanese shoe manufacturer had gone so well.
So he wrote to them to find out what was going on with the samples he'd been promised, which he'd paid $50 for.
He then got a letter back saying, shoes coming in just a little more days.
Phil was back at his parents house, and so he showed the letter to his dad, who just chuckled and said, son, that 50 bucks is long gone.
Had Phil really been scammed?
Depressed, Phil went and got a job to try and make some money.
He ended up working as an accountant, but he didn't really like it.
And then suddenly one morning, 12 sample pairs of shoes from Japan arrived on his doorstep.
They were finally here, and it was worth the wait.
They were just like he'd hoped.
Phil was so excited that he went to see his old running coach Bill Bowerman to show him the new shoes and see what he thought.
Bowerman was highly respected in the world of running, and he'd always been obsessed with improving athletes' shoes.
In fact, back when Phil was at university with him, he'd notice Bowerman take students' shoes and cut them open and make adjustments.
For example, adding more cushion or using more lightweight materials and then stitching them back together.
Sometimes his experiments just made their feet painful, but quite often, Bowerman improved the shoes and made them better or more comfortable for running.
One thing was for sure, Bowerman really knew his stuff when it came to running shoes, and that's why Phil had been so keen to hear his opinion on his new Japanese running shoes.
Surprisingly, Bowerman liked the sample shoes so much that he offered to be Phil's business partner.
And Bowerman was basically the perfect partner to have.
He'd spent his life on the track training athlete, was one of the most experienced track coaches with countless records and he was obsessed with the construction of track shoes.
So Phil and Babelman agreed to be co-founders of this new company, Blue Ribbon Sports, with both of them investing $500 each into their new company.
And all that money was used to order 300 pairs of shoes from Japan at a price of roughly $3.33 per pair.
Phil also wrote a letter to Onitsuka asking if Blue Ribbon Sports could be the exclusive distributor of these Tiger shoes in the western United States.
They agreed and shortly after, in In April 1964, a shipment of 300 Tiger shoes arrived from Japan.
Phil now had a shoe supplier, a business partner and hundreds of shoes to sell.
There was just one problem.
What Phil didn't have was anywhere to sell the shoes.
You see, when Phil went to all of the local sporting goods stores to see if they'd stock the shoe, they didn't take Phil seriously, and they said they had no need for another track shoe.
So, Phil realised he was going to have to sell these shoes himself.
Phil had 300 pairs of shoes to sell, so he began going to track meets and running clubs and started selling the shoes from the trunk of his car.
He would enthusiastically show the shoes to runners, coaches and fans at the running track.
His commitment and drive, together with Bowerman's connections, saw them sell out all 300 pairs within just 3 months.
It was interesting, because in the past when Phil had tried sales, he'd failed horribly, but that was when he was selling encyclopedias door to door.
When it came to these running shoes, selling them seemed strangely easy, and Phil felt that was because customers could sense his personal belief in the product.
His conviction that these shoes genuinely were better than alternatives made people want to buy them.

Plus, clearly there was demand for these high quality shoes at an affordable price, as by the end of their first year, Blue Ribbon Sports had sold $8,000 worth of shoes, and so Phil used the money he'd made to order 900 more pairs from Japan.
Shortly after this, they recruited some sales reps, mostly ex-runners who shared their vision of what the company was trying to do, and who solely worked on commission.
They'd get $2 for every pair of shoes they sold, and so they drove all over America to every high school and college track meet they could.
This success allowed Phil to get a business loan from the bank, so they could move Blue Ribbon Sports out of Phil's parents' basement and into its first real office.

However, since Bowerman still had a full-time job, Phil decided to hire the company's first full-time employee, Jeff Johnson, the man who would later go on to come up with the company's iconic name, Nike.
But for now, they were still called Blue Ribbon Sports.
And with sales rising rapidly, in 1966 they were able to open their own retail store to sell their shoes.

Clever move they made was they designed the store to be a sanctuary for runners, a place they could hang out and talk, and browse shelves full of books related to running, which helped them attract a lot of attention to the store.
And whilst Phil and the new employee Johnson and worked on the business side of the operations, Bowerman was handling the creative side of things.
For example, Bowerman began to tinker with the shoe designs.
Once a shipment arrived from Japan, he would take a few shoes and rip them apart to see how they were designed.
Once he'd studied the shoe, he would make notes on how to improve them.
These notes were then sent to the manufacturer in Japan, asking for changes to be made before the next shipment.
You could say that Bowerman was basically now designing Onitsuka's shoes for them.
Around this time, Bowerman also started coaching popular runners and future Olympians, helping to build their brand further and sell even more shoes.
And not just that, but Bauman almost single-handedly made jogging popular.
You see, back in the 60s, jogging was not a mainstream exercise at all, but Bauman wrote a book about it that surprisingly sold over a million copies, and helped kickstart the popularity of jogging.
Which of course meant more people were in need of jogging shoes, and what better place to buy them than the company of the man who'd popularised jogging in the first place.
In fact, one of Bauman's shoe designs, called the Cortez, became the highest selling shoe in 1969, with Blue Ribbon making a total revenue of around $300,000.
So, business was booming, and everything seemed to be going great between Phil's company Blue Ribbon Sports and Onitsuka in Japan.
Together, they'd created a partnership that brought success to both parties.
But what Phil didn't know, was that Onitsuka was planning to stab them in the back.
Phil asked Onitsuka if Blue Ribbon Sports could be the exclusive distributor for Tiger Shoes across all of America, not just the West like previously agreed.
But they initially said no, because they didn't think Phil's company was big or established enough to handle that, and they wanted someone with offices on the East Coast.
On the spot, Phil immediately said, but we do have offices on the East Coast.
In reality, they didn't.
But Onitsuka believed Phil, and was impressed that Blue Ribbon seemed like a much bigger company than they'd initially realised.
So they struck a deal for Blue Ribbon to be the exclusive US partner for the Tiger brand shoes, and Phil ordered 20,000 more pairs.
The executive from Onitsuka told them he'd shipped them to Blue Ribbon's East Coast office, which of course, they didn't really have.
So after the meeting, to try and raise money for these new offices, Phil sent out flyers advertising the chance for people to invest in Blue Ribbon Sports.
They said it was a fast growing shoe company looking to expand and people could buy shares.
They then sat back and waited for people to invest.
But nobody at all responded.
It was humiliating, and also extremely worrying that nobody seemed to believe in the potential of their business, as nobody at all wanted to invest their money.
The only money they did get was from the parents of one of Blue Ribbon's early employees, Bob Waddell.
His parents knew the company desperately needed cash and offered to put in $8,000, which was literally their entire life savings.
It drained their balance to almost zero and put them in a very difficult financial situation, but they wanted to do what they could to give the company the best chance of survival.
Phil didn't want to take their money, but the banks were refusing to loan him anymore, and so he had no other real choice.
On the plus side, Phil and Bowerman both loved the shoes created by Onitsuka.

They respected the quality of the Japanese brand, and of course it seemed win-win for both sides, because thanks to their company Blue Ribbon Sports, Onitsuka had now become a formidable brand in the United States.
So Phil understandably thought that the future of his company was with Onitsuka, but the truth is, they had some problems, and they were about to get even bigger.

You see, the initial success of Blue Ribbon Sports had led to the rapid opening of new stores, which often left Phil in a risky situation where he constantly had to worry about cash flow to support the increase in stores and employees.
Phil had to get more facilities, hire more staff and order more shoes.
The Cortez for example had quickly become one of the most popular shoes in America, and they were selling out faster than they could keep up with.
So Phil repeatedly tried to have Onitsuka send the shoes faster to meet the demand, but the Japanese brand continued to send them at the same pace.
It was only later that Phil found out that Onitsuka had been selling to their Japanese customers first as their priority, and simply importing whatever was left over to the US.
It was unfair, but there wasn't really much Phil could do.

To compound the situation, Onitsuka was slow to produce the suggestions and innovations that Phil and Bowerman shared with them, and sometimes they completely ignored their suggestions, which infuriated Bowerman who'd been working hard on new designs and improvements.
So, hoping to improve the situation with their supplier and discuss renewing their contract, Phil arranged another in-person meeting with a representative from Onitsuka, a man named Kitami.
But the meeting was strange, Kitami said Blue Ribbon sales were disappointing, and didn't seem that interested in renewing a long-term deal with Blue Ribbon.
Phil couldn't understand it.
He felt his company had definitely earned the contract extension.
After all, Onitsuka's success in the United States was down to Blue Ribbon Sports.
They'd introduced the Tiger brand in America, and sales were growing every year.
Phil even showed them a survey that revealed that 70% of American runners wore or owned one of their shoes.
Not to mention that Bauman had helped improve their shoe designs.
Phil had already been a little suspicious that Onitsuka was planning to make partnerships with other distributors, and it was becoming increasingly clear that something wasn't right.
So when Kitami left the room, Phil took a folder out of his briefcase.
It contained a list of 18 athletic shoe distributors across the US, and a schedule of appointments to meet with them.
It was now clear that Onitsuka was secretly plotting to replace Blue Ribbon and find a new distributor.

From their perspective, now that they'd gained a significant foothold in the United States, thanks to Blue Ribbon's efforts, the Onitsuka executives decided that they needed to move on to more experienced distributors to expand and increase their revenue.
Phil was outraged, but most of all, he was hurt.
He confronted them about this and pointed out they still had a contract in place for at least another year.
However, the Japanese brand then gave Phil an ultimatum.
Either we buy 51% of Blue Ribbon Sports, or otherwise, we make deals with other distribution partners.
Phil Knight immediately rejected their offer to buy his company.
He didn't want to sell, and he couldn't believe this was happening.
But Phil knew there was really only one way forward now.
If Onitsuka was going to start partnering with other American distributors, then it was time for war.
It took a little while for Phil to get over the shock of everything that had gone down in the meeting, but when he did, he decided to strike back.
Phil and Bowerman realised that losing the Onitsuka Tiger brand wasn't necessarily the end of the world.
In fact, maybe this was an opportunity.
They could be so much more than just a distributor.
After After all, the Cortez, Onitsuka's best selling shoe, was Bauman's design.
So why couldn't Blue Ribbon just make their own shoes and sell them?
Plus, that way, they wouldn't have to keep waiting for shipments to arrive, and they could make as many shoes as they wanted.
So the two co-founders gathered the whole team together and began working on creating their own original shoes, instead of selling Onitsuka's Tiger shoes.
But first, they needed a new name.
Phil initially wanted to call their new brand Dimension 6, but pretty much nobody else liked that name.
And then Jeff Johnson, their first employee, said an idea had suddenly come to him in a dream the previous night.
Let's call it Nike.
Phil just looked at him blankly and said, what?
It's the Greek wing goddess of victory, Johnson explained.
Phil thought back to the temple he'd visited whilst travelling.
He had to admit, the connection to victory certainly made a lot of sense for a sports brand.
But the truth was that Phil himself actually wasn't that keen on the name Nike at first.
But the problem was, they were running out of time and had to decide on a name right now, because they needed to start making plans for their new shoe brand as soon as possible.
So, left with few other options, Phil agreed to go with the name Nike.
Next up, they needed a logo.
So, they recruited a graphic design student from a nearby university to create it, and she came up with the now iconic swoosh.
She got paid just $35 for it.
But now that the name and logo were sorted out, there was one more crucial thing they needed to do to really take the fight to Onitsuka.
Phil needed a shoe manufacturer who could produce their new high quality shoes at an affordable price.

They already had the design they wanted to use for their first shoe with the Nike logo, which was basically a new version of the popular Cortez, but they had to find the right manufacturer to make it.
And all the initial manufacturers they tested seemed to have quality control issues.
At a company meeting, Phil told his employees, our partnership with Onitsuka is over, and we're completely on our own now.
We have this new line we're working on now which we're calling Nike, but there are big problems with the quality.
We're trying to get it fixed, but we don't have much time, so there's no margin for error.

Phil looked down the table at the employees in the meeting, and realised everyone was slumped in their seats, looking defeated, as if losing their deal with Onitsuka meant the end of Blue Ribbon Sports.
Phil realised he needed to inspire his team, and so he pivoted his speech, and said, so in other words, this is the moment we've been waiting for.
Everyone around the table looked up, and Phil continued, no more selling someone else's brand.

Onitsuka has been holding us down for years, their late deliveries, their mixed up orders, their refusal to hear and implement our design ideas, let's not look at this as a crisis, let's look at this as our liberation."
As Phil stopped speaking, he could sense a wave of relief around the table.
The mood had changed after Phil's speech, and the employees felt that maybe, just maybe, this wasn't the end of the company at all.
They all got to work on how they could make this new Nike brand successful, and how they could partner with the right manufacturers.

Although Phil made sure he didn't make the same mistake he'd made with Onitsuka, so rather than committing to just one manufacturer, he established a network of manufacturers which gave him full control over production.

That wasn't quite the end of their dealings with Onitsuka though, as they actually sued Blue Ribbon Sports, claiming starting this new Nike brand breached their contract which stated Blue Ribbon would only sell Tiger shoes.
Phil then countersued that Onitsuka had actively been trying to break its exclusivity deal with Blue Ribbon Sports, and in the end both parties eventually settled and went their separate ways.
In 1971, the company Blue Ribbon Sports officially became Nike, and by this point the company crossed a million dollars in sales per year.
And from then onwards, Nike's expansion skyrocketed as they began to grow into the most famous sports brand we know and recognise today.
At the 1972 Olympics, Nike featured heavily, giving them a lot of exposure on a global stage.
Revenue rapidly rose to $14 million in 1976, and then doubled in just one year to $28 million in 1977.
Around that time, Phil opened new factories around the world and continued to reinvest everything in more growth.
And it was working.
Nike was on a huge upswing.
They weren't only gaining market share, but they were also fast becoming a fashion statement.
However, their success was being envied by a lot of American brands, who were watching very closely, waiting for the moment to strike the company down.
Things seemed to be going great for Nike.
Sales were amazing, word of mouth was positive, and their legal disputes were behind them.
The only slight problem was they were actually still quite cash poor.
Phil was reinvesting every penny he could back into more growth, and even borrowing money to help ramp up expansion faster.
To him, it was grow or die, so he kept ordering more and more shoes, opening more stores and hiring more employees.
To help fund this expansion, Phil was thinking about taking the company public, but then one morning he got a letter that changed everything.
It was a bill from the US Customs Service saying Nike owed them $25 million.
At first, Phil thought it must be a joke or some strange mistake.
If they actually did owe $25 million to the government, they'd be out of business.
It would all be over just like that, everything they'd worked for.
After a few phone calls, it soon became clear that the bill was completely real, and the actual reason behind it was something surprisingly sinister.
What had happened was that Nike's American competitors, Keds, Converse and a few small factories, were getting scared of Nike's popularity and growth.

They saw Nike as a threat that could potentially shut them out of the market, so they'd sent representatives to Washington and lobbied the customs office to effectively put a stop to Nike's growth by enforcing something called American selling price.

ASP was an archaic rule from before the Great Depression, that said if there was a shoe manufactured by a company in the US, then anyone importing a similar shoe from abroad must pay an import duty of 20% of the competitor's selling price.

The whole idea behind this law was to promote nationalism, and essentially prevent companies from importing products that could be made in America, and Nike's competitors had lobbied the federal government to enforce this old rule.
You see, because Nike wasn't manufacturing its shoes in America, but in Japan, their competitors realised all they needed to do was make a copy of Nike's shoes and make them extremely expensive.

By doing that, they had successfully created an American alternative, and even though Nike's shoes were the original thing, because Nike's products were being imported from another country, they got hit with the ridiculously high import fees because of this American selling price rule.

This basically meant Phil would have to pay an additional $6 on every pair they imported, To make matters much worse, the import duties were backdated three years on every pair of shoes Nike had imported, which ultimately had led to the $25 million bill they received.
Phil knew there was no way Nike could pay that much money, it would bankrupt them.
There was only one option, and that was to fight.
Phil hired one of the best lawyers he could find, and for three brutal years, Phil went neck and neck with the customs office and the likes of Converse and Keds in court.
Nike also produced a TV commercial telling their story and explaining what was happening to them, to try and get customers fired up and on their side.
And it worked.

Nike's competitors and their accomplices in the government realised Nike were going to fight this with everything they had, and in the end they reached a settlement of $9 million instead of $25 million.

Phil still thought this was outrageous, but in those 3 years the legal battle had been going on, Nike had grown tremendously, and their sales had reached a whopping $440 million, so they could now afford to settle and put the whole thing behind them.
It had been another close scare, but the company had now made it through stronger than ever, and now it was time for some very good news.
In 1980 Nike became a public company, which effectively killed its cash flow problems completely and allowed them to ramp up their growth even more.
And since Phil alone owned a 46% share of the company, he became a very wealthy man.
But also, remember earlier on the parents of one of Nike's early employees invested their life savings into helping the company survive when they were low on cash?
Well they hadn't done that as an investment to make money at all, they'd simply done it to try and keep the company alive.
But they'd been given shares in return.
And so after Nike went public, Phil had one of the happiest moments of his career, when he got to tell them their initial $8,000 investment was now worth $1.6 million.
That money was obviously completely life changing for them and they couldn't believe it.
From there on, Nike became bigger and bigger.
Phil signed deals with two Chinese factories which made Nike the first American shoemaker to be allowed to do business in China.

They also branched out into selling clothes, and this not only helped them make more money and attract more investors, but it also gave them an advantage when negotiating endorsement deals with athletes, as they could now offer them more than just shoes.
And celebrity endorsements were actually one of Nike's biggest keys to success.

They agreed deals with rookie athletes like Tiger Woods and LeBron James in the very early stages of their career, and of course when they went on to become massive stars, it massively boosted Nike's popularity.
Although their most lucrative endorsement of all was with Michael Jordan.

They spotted his potential early on and signed him for a sponsorship deal back in the beginning of his career, and as Jordan rose to stardom, his shoe line, Air Jordan's, went on to make hundreds of millions of dollars.
By 1986, Nike had overtaken Converse to become the biggest sports brand in America.
And at this point, you might be thinking that Nike is simply an incredible business success story.
But here's the thing, behind all that success was a very dark secret.
A secret that involved violent intimidation, slavery, harassment and child labour.
And that secret was about to be exposed.
It was 1991, and everyone working at Nike was having a normal day, when American labor activist Jeffrey Ballinger published a report that nearly destroyed Nike's entire reputation.
In his film Behind the Swoosh, he claimed that Nike secretly used child labour, and that the company exploited people living in underdeveloped countries.
The video claimed that workers in these countries were forced to live in slums, or near open sewers where they shared toilets and bathwater with over 100 different families.
These workers were then cramped in factories which were often housed in damaged buildings that post fire risks.

During their work hours, they were denied access to drinking water or toilets, and at the end of the day, after which they'd gone through all this inhumane treatment, they were paid a meagre sum of $1.25.
Then, in 2001, a BBC documentary uncovered use of child labour and poor working conditions in a Cambodian factory used by Nike.
The document focused on 6 girls who all worked 7 days a week, often 16 hours a day.
All of these claims led to a lot of backlash, with many students and activists around the world participating in protests against Nike.
Some people called for a boycott of all their products, and several universities cut ties with the shoe brand completely.
Sales dropped and Nike's stock fell by 15%, with the company being portrayed in the media as a company willing to exploit workers and deprive them of their basic wages needed to sustain themselves.
Phil Knight had always been in a position where him and his company were the good guys, but this time he was the bad guy.
It was a different challenge, and he responded by promising he would personally ensure conditions at Nike factories improved around the world.
After that Nike spent the next decade trying to fix its reputation.
Of course, the truth is, the company was basically founded on the principle of finding cheaper labour abroad in order to be able to make good quality shoes that were cheaper than competitors.
But to be fair, Nike definitely did make changes to significantly improve conditions for overseas workers, and many human rights activists have acknowledged their efforts to minimise these problems.
But allegations never fully stopped.

A 2005 report by the company found that workers in up to half of its factories were still forced to work 60 hour weeks, made less than minimum wage or were denied the use of bathrooms and drinking water.

And even more recently, in December 2021, the European Centre for Constitutional and Human Rights filed a criminal complaint against Nike and other brands, alleging that they benefited from the use of forced labour in China.
Now, to be fair and give the other side to this, Phil would argue that those factories involved in these scandals weren't actually Nikes, they just rented them along with other tenants.
So Nike wasn't directly controlling these factories, they just made deals with them.

And whilst that's not an excuse, Phil is right that singling out Nike for using sweatshops misses the bigger picture, which is that countless multinational companies use overseas labour with very questionable conditions in parts of their supply chains.
Many of the items we all use every day were quite possibly produced with cheap labour in terrible working conditions.
If making videos for this channel has taught me anything, it's that if you look into almost any business deep enough, you're gonna find a darker side.
But what's particularly interesting about Nike, is how they've managed to turn controversy into profits.
In 2018, Nike launched a new ad titled Dream Crazy, with former NFL player Colin Kaepernick as the voice and face of its new Just Do It campaign.
Kaepernick himself posted a black and white close up photo of his face with the words, believe in something, even if it means sacrificing everything.

That statement was in reference to a controversy that began back in 2016, when Kaepernick himself triggered a political scandal by kneeling during the US national anthem to protest against racial injustice and police brutality in America.
Many people, including then President Donald Trump, claimed that Kaepernick was disrespecting the flag and the country.
So Nike's partnership with Colin was controversial to say the least.
Their stock price immediately fell 2.5% and many people across the United States destroyed their Nike shoes and declared a boycott of the company.
But then, something interesting happened.
A lot of people who shared the same sentiment behind the theme of Nike's ad came on their side, and many people started buying and wearing Nike's products as a show of support.

Thanks to the controversial and bold marketing move, Nike got more attention than ever and broke many records, gaining $6 billion in brand value, 163 million in media, and an additional 31% bump in sales.
The campaign also earned Nike its first Emmy award since 2002 for the most outstanding commercial of 2019.
In the end, all the shouts for the boycott of Nike products had little significance or any major impact on its sales.
And this wasn't the first time that Nike had leaned into controversies to make more money.
In 1988, Nike released its first Just Do It campaign.
The campaign touched on the subject of ageism, featuring an 80 year old marathon runner who ran 17 miles every morning.
Then in February 1995, Nike released a Just Do It campaign which featured a HIV positive runner.
So why does Nike take risks in their ads that they know will create some controversy?
Well the reality is, Nike have an experienced marketing team that assess the risk vs reward, and makes a calculated decision.
In the case of ads like these, they weighed up the costs and believed that the benefits were worth it.
And whilst many other factors obviously affect sales, it's clear that their ad campaigns have played a huge role in the company's success.
Between when the first Jest Do It campaign launched in 1988 to 1998, Nike increased sales from $800 million to $9.2 billion.

title: Papa John's: Scandals, Betrayal & Dumpster Diving
note: Scrappy underdog rise with a mid-film sponsor read, followed by a late fall caused by the founder himself.
sections: Teen pizza cook and college dream
Saving Mick's Lounge and the broom closet
Building the first pizzeria; father dies
lines: Papa John's has over 5,500 locations globally, revenues reported at over $2 billion, and is one of the most successful pizza fast food chains in the world.

And so, it may be hard to believe that Papa John's started out of a barroom's broom closet, that its founder resorted to dumpster diving in the hopes of finding more customers, or that the fate of the company was decided over a speedboat.
This is the untold truth of Papa John's Pizza, and the Papa who made it all happen.

It was the autumn of 1977 in Jeffersonville, Indiana, when a young 15-year-old kid by the name of John Hate Shatner got his first job washing dishes at a small Italian pizzeria known as Rocky's Sub-Pub.
But John wasn't content with just washing dishes, and set his sights on making pizzas from his first day.

After months of hard work, the Fondrisi family who owned the restaurant allowed John to start occasionally preparing the pizza dough and tomato sauce, but they adamantly kept the honour of baking pizzas within the family.
Still, John refused to give up and persevered, and his determination paid off a couple of months later when Rockies was given a glowing review by Kentucky's largest newspaper.
As a result, the restaurant became so busy that same night that the Fondrises were forced to ask John to help bake pizzas to keep up with the demand.
Despite only ever watching the family make pizzas, he took to it like a fish to water, and never went back to dishwashing again.
Then, after graduating high school, John attended Bell State University, pursuing a degree in business administration.
Whilst attending college, he needed a job to cover his tuition and living expenses, but a brief yet miserable stint working at Wendy's scared John away from ever flipping burgers again.
Instead, he decided to return to pizza making at the college town's local pizzeria named Greeks.
The owner took John under his wing and showed him how to efficiently handle high volume orders and maximise productivity.
In fact, John loved working at Greeks so much that he was tempted to drop out of school and start a Greeks franchise, but his mother and grandfather convinced him to finish his degree.
Still, the idea of running a pizza chain stuck with him, and as he completed his university classes, he began dreaming up his own pizzeria.
However, by now it was 1982, and chains like Pizza Hut, Domino's and Little Caesars were well on their way to taking over America.
If John wanted to stand a chance against these growing giants, he needed to come up with a way to stand out from the competition.
Ultimately, John figured that if Pizza Hut owned variety, Domino's owned speed, and Little Caesar's own price, the only place left to compete was in taste and quality.
Looking towards his experiences at Greeks, he decided that his pizzeria chain needed to look, feel and taste like a mom and pop pizza shop no matter how big it got.
Afterwards, John toiled away in his free time, designing menus, sketching out floor plans, writing out recipes, figuring out what equipment he would need and so on.
But he was stumped on what to call his dream pizzeria though.
John turned to one of his college dorm mates majoring in marketing and asked if he could come up with a name and logo for him.
Just a few days later, he was handed a logo that read Papa John's.
It was exactly what he wanted.
Unfortunately, he didn't have enough funding yet, so his dreams and plans would be packaged away in a cardboard box in his closet for a few more years.
After graduating, John moved back home to Jeffersonville, but he had difficulties finding work.
After unsuccessfully applying for dozens of jobs, John's father Robert approached him with an offer to manage a tavern he owned named Mix Lounge.
The catch was that the bar was falling apart, the quality of the drink and food were rock bottom, employee morale was awful, and worst of all, the business was $64,000 in debt.
Robert believed the place was doomed, and hoped his son John could minimise the damage so that he wouldn't be left completely bankrupt.
Despite the grim outlook, John was ecstatic to take on the challenge, and worked tirelessly over the next 7 months to save the bar.
Given free reign, John's entrepreneurial spirit went wild as he came up with cost-cutting measures, creative sales techniques, and events to drive at profits.
He even sold off his beloved 1971 Chevrolet Camaro to pay off the business's debts in time.
By the end of February 1984 John achieved the seemingly impossible.
He transformed Mix into a successful bar.
As amazing and gratifying as this achievement was, John soon realised he wasn't truly happy.
While he loved running his own business, he had no love for running a bar in particular.
The constant stench of alcohol and smoke, alongside the nightly bar brawls, took its toll.
John swore, I didn't want that life, and I didn't want to be complicit in helping others live it either.
I had to find something else, something actually fulfilling.
One fateful night in March 1984, John's gaze fell upon a broom closet while he was closing up Mix.
It suddenly came to him in a flash.
His dreams of running his own pizzeria could start right here.
After all, he made a fine profit serving up bar food to customers in Mix already, why not start serving up pizzas instead?
He went home, immediately dug the cardboard box filled with his Papa John's plans out of his closet and began plotting away.
The next morning, John gathered Robert and the team at Mix to excitedly pitch them his idea of working their way out of the bar business and running a pizza company instead.
After seeing what his son had achieved with Mix, Robert signed on at once and the others quickly followed suit.
They wasted no time getting started and began tearing down the broom closet's outer walls to make room for a pizza oven that very same night.
Within a couple of weeks, split between renovating the broom closet while still running Mix as usual, John and his team had everything ready to get their humble, very cramped pizzeria underway.
way.

With the profits from the bar covering John's overhead and expenses, he spent the next few months baking away in the tavern's broom closet turned pizzeria, improving his skills, since he'd become a little rusty after not making pizzas in years.
He shared his early creations with his employees and the bar's customers, using that as a focus group to figure out what worked and what didn't.
After finally finding his pizza making groove, John ran into another snag.
It turned out it wasn't easy to gain customers when your pizzeria is based out the back of a bar.
He tried passing town, sending out coupons, running newspaper ads and more, but nothing really worked.
And that's when John came up with a devious scheme.
Late at night John snuck over to the pizza delivery king of the town, Domino's.
His target?
Their dumpster, which contained hundreds of receipt slips with customers names, addresses and orders.
John happily dived into the dumpster and stole as many receipts as he could.
After collecting enough from his dumpster database, John wrote each potential customer a personally signed letter which read, To the pizza lover who this concerns, Papa John's makes better pizzas.
We'll give you half off on your first order.
Give us a try.
It was dirty business, literally.
But it worked extremely well.
Sales massively increased.
Eventually the Domino's caught on and soaked their receipts in water before tossing them out to stop him.
But by then it was too late.
Papa John's had a loyal and growing customer base and was finally on the road to success.
This was a big deal.
Word was spreading throughout the town about John's new up and coming pizza joint, but there was yet another problem.
Nearly all of their business was made via delivery, as whenever new customers came to mix in person for a Papa John's pizza, they rarely, if ever, came back.
Whilst John had done his best to spruce up mix, there was no change in the fact it was a bar, far from the mom and pop family restaurant he'd always wanted Papa John's to be.
So in February 1985, John took out a $40,000 loan to erect the first proper Papa John's pizzeria.
Luckily he didn't even have to look hard for a location, as right next to their bar was a boarded up KFC that had since moved away years ago, which had all the space they needed.
After cleaning out the space, John and his crew created handmade miniature paper scale models of their future restaurant to be.
They settled on a design, but came to the realisation they wouldn't be able to afford hiring construction workers, forcing John and his team to do all the work themselves.
All the while, they still ran Mick's bar and the pizzeria in its broom closet, as they needed every cent they earned to fund the construction.
It was grueling work.
Mick's often became John's home as he sweated it out till the early hours of the morning and passed out in a corner of the tavern before waking up and starting all over again.
After six weeks of non-stop labour, they were almost done, but tragedy was right around the corner.
In mid-March 1985, John's father checked into hospital.
At first, his illness didn't seem too serious, but his health rapidly deteriorated.
Five days later, Robert Shatner passed away, leaving John devastated.
Nevertheless, the morning following his father's funeral, John was determined to still make his father proud.
He hurried over to Mix, entered and paused.
On his right stood the bar, and on his left remained the incomplete Papa John's.
He looked back and forth between the two.
He could have easily taken a seat at the bar and drowned his sorrows away.
No one would have blamed him for it.
The man's father he was so close with had suddenly died.
But he refused.
He knew his father would have wanted him to finish building the pizzeria and see his dream come true.
He turned to the left, picked up a hammer and some nails, and went back to work.

On April 11th, 1985, just 19 days after his father's passing, and around a year after John first began making pizzas out of Mick's broom closet, the first proper Papa John's restaurant opened its doors for business.

Although they were located right next to Mick's, their business improved exponentially, both due to the more family-friendly atmosphere, as well as the simple fact of having the Papa John's logo proudly displayed on a sign above the door, rather than hidden away in the back of a bar.
At the end of their first month, they'd tripled their previous sales record inside Mix, and their growth only continued from there.
By the next month, they eclipsed the sales of their toughest competitor, the dominoes John had dumped a dive at before.
That got John thinking, if he could beat the competition in Jeffersonville, then what was stopping him from taking on the rest of the world?
As the revenues of their first location grew each week, John turned to the task of figuring out where to open his second location.
Not wanting to stretch himself too far, especially given the shockingly fast-paced his business was growing, he chose the nearby town of Clarksville, Indiana.
It was just around 5 miles away and right outside of their current delivery range.
This idea of building new locations just a little further away from their previous locations became a key tactic of the business's future.
John figured that building locations outwards from one another breeds a stronger community compared to randomly opening locations far and wide from one another.
John was also careful to learn from his first restaurant before blindly building another.
The original Papa John's next to Mix included a full dining room complete with fine tableware and an expanded menu.
It fitted John's dream of a mom and pop style restaurant, but the numbers showed that most of his customers preferred carryout or delivery rather than dining in.
Unafraid of admitting that times were changing and ever quick to adapt, John cut the fat when designing his second location.
The interior and menu was simplified and it was built off of a local highway to better facilitate the pick up and go nature of the business.
Leading up to the second location's grand opening, John returned to his old tricks and raided the dumpster of Clarksville's Domino's for customer addresses to send handwritten letters to.
It worked just as well as before, and sales at Clarksville's Papa John's grew every week that went by.
Unwilling to let the momentum go to waste, John quickly set off on building a third location in the next town over, less than a month later, which proved to be yet another success.
John's aggressive tactics were evidently working, so on December 1st 1986, he decided to open a location in the nearby city of Louisville, Kentucky.
Unfortunately, their beginner's luck in the relatively sleepy bergs of southern Indiana hit a brick wall when entering Kentucky's biggest city.
The Domino's here was well entrenched thanks to their mutual relationship with Louisville's downtown hotel industry.
It was disappointing seeing his winning streak come to an end, but John refused to close their struggling Louisville location.
Instead, John turned his attention towards upgrading the infrastructure of his pizza chain.
And additionally, John also took care to put people who shared his vision of Papa John's future in charge of each of his locations, and then stepped aside as they went to work.
This hands-off approach left him free to focus on the long-term success of the company.
Then, in 1987, the Papa John's location in Louisville finally broke through, earning a profit and a dedicated following.

Thanks to the time John spent improving the company's foundation, he was able to capitalize on this success with vengeance and bought out three locations of a failed pizza chain in the city to be converted to Papa John's as well.
Meanwhile, John also saw his dreams of turning Papa John's into a franchise finally come true too.
Their first franchisees were actually prior Domino's owners who were convinced to defect to Papa John's side after seeing the young chain's success.
And before long, more and more people flocked to open their own Papa John's franchise.
Not everyone agreed with John's vision.
After Robert's passing, Papa John's ownership was split between three people.
John personally owned 49%, one of his earliest team members Bob Erringer owned 36%, and John's Uncle Bill owned 15%.
The trio had an excellent relationship during the company's early years, each contributing as much as they could, but things began to sour by 1987.
The key issue became that despite all of Papa John's successes, none of them were receiving much in the way of profits.
John was adamant about reinvesting every single cent they earned back into the company to further fuel its growth, which was clearly paying off, but Bill didn't see things that way.
Bill was in his 60s by now, and didn't understand why they needed to work so hard, especially when he wasn't seeing a dime of it.
He wanted to stop spending so much money, time and effort on expanding.
As he saw it, Papa John's was big enough already, so why not just kick back and cash in the checks for a change?
To make matters worse, Bill spent a great deal of time driving around with Bob maintaining the stores, and used that time to slowly but surely bring him over to his side rather than John's.
Things finally came to a head when one of the trio's weekly meetings devolved into a vicious argument.
Neither John nor Bill was willing to back down, and Bob, tired of working day in and day out for years, took Bill's side.
Together the pair represented 51% of the company, which was all that was needed to throw the fate of Papa John's into question.

John recognised he needed to regain control of his company and fast, otherwise his life's work could come crashing down, especially as the infighting was already causing the chain's quality control to slip.
But the question was how?
Then in early 1988, Bob called up John, asking for $20,000.
Bob had become obsessed with the speed belt he'd purchased and wanted to increase its power with a new muffler.
John saw his chance and offered to hand over the cash in exchange for 2% of Bob's shares in Papa John's.
Bob agreed to that, But this meant that John now owned a majority in the company, and thus, Papa John's future was saved.
All thanks to a speedboat muffler.
Later that year, John decided to buy out their shares completely for over $300,000.
That probably seemed like a fine prize to Bob and Bill at the time.
Although, they would soon look back and think, they'd got ripped off.
Now that John had full control of the business, he was free to take his company to a whole new level.
By the end of the 1980s, there were nearly 40 Papa John's restaurants.
Yet by June 10th 1991, Papa John's celebrated the opening of its 100th location.
That number doubled the very next year, as Papa John's spread further out towards lucrative metropolitan markets such as Indianapolis, Cincinnati, Nashville, Cleveland, Memphis, St.
Louis, Atlanta and more.
Still, despite their victories, John's ambitions were running faster than his profits.
That's when Rick Sherman, the CEO of Rally's hamburger chain, suggested that John use Wall Street's money to further fund Papa John's growth.
After months of seemingly endless paperwork, Papa John's hit Wall Street on June 8th 1993.
Wall Street brokers instantly fell in love with the chain and snatched up its stocks like crazy.
In a single day, Papa John's became worth $344 million.
Less than 10 years since it started, Papa John's had finally entered the big leagues and its ascent only continued from there.
In 1998, Papa John's first international location opened in Mexico City and the chain reported $1 billion in system-wide restaurant sales.
In 1999, Papa John's had 2,000 restaurants to its name.
In 2002, Papa John's broke ground by becoming the first pizza chain to allow online ordering across all of its domestic locations.
This paid off dividends as the company's online sales topped $1 billion alone in 2008.
Finally, in 2016, John Soror's Pizza Chain surpassed 5,000 locations worldwide.
But let's pause.

If you are someone who loves a Disney-style fairytale ending, this is the point to click off the video, because unfortunately, this incredible rags to riches story from Broom Cupboard to one of the world's largest pizza chains would end in controversy.
In 2017, Papa John's hit a rough patch.
Pizza sales were down, and so was their stock price.
But John came out and blamed the NFL for this, which Papa John's was the sponsor of.
John publicly criticized the NFL for its handling of the national anthem protests started by Colin Kaepernick to draw attention to police brutality and racial inequality.
His comments were very poorly received, as they not only seemed to be passing the blame, but also insensitive to the issues involved.
So executives at the company hired a firm to help train John to handle the media better in future, and avoid any more public backlash.

However, in an extremely ironic turn of events, during a call with the PR firm, John used the n-word, was trying to explain why he didn't think his comments were that bad compared to what other people had said.
After this, the PR company immediately stopped working with him.
And when the media found out why, and John's comments got leaked, it created lots more headlines of controversy for Papa John's.
All the backlash from this meant that John stepped down as CEO and chairman of the company.
To distance themselves further from John, Papa John's began removing his face from ads and packaging.
Papa John's headquarters then cancelled the sublease agreement on John's office, effectively evicting the founder of the company from his own office.

Papa John's also created a new policy, which was dubbed a poison pill, that ensures John can never acquire a controlling stake in his own company again, since he was considered too toxic to the brand.
Of course, that's not ideal when the company is literally named after him.
For John, he felt like he'd been betrayed by his own company.
In November 2019, John finally did a public interview to address everything, and went on to criticise Papa John's and the way it had been run since his departure.

He even criticised the company's food, saying, I've had over 40 pizzas in the last 30 days, and it's not the same pizza, it's not the same He ended by warning that the company's day of reckoning will come.

title: The Craziest CEO Ever: War, Drugs & Time Machines
note: Boom-and-bust biography with a war-zone factory and a sting; cultural afterlife and revival come after the company's death.
sections: Pontiac GTO to Chevrolet, Vega, exit from GM
Founding DMC and the car design
Factory in Northern Ireland and the Troubles
Back to the Future time machine
Parts, replicas and revival; DeLorean's death
lines: The DeLorean car was made famous thanks to the Back to the Future movies, but the real company that made DeLoreans went bankrupt within just a couple of years of starting.
So what happened?
The crazy story of DeLorean involves a war, FBI agents, and a million dollar drug deal gone wrong.
It's a business story with a meteoric rise to the top and a disastrous fall to the bottom, with lots of wealth, fame and drama along the way, plus a very eccentric CEO.
But in true DeLorean style, to make sense of all of this, we need to travel back in time.
Our story starts in the 1920s in Detroit, Michigan, the mecca of America's auto industry and home of the big three.
Ford, General Motors and Chrysler all proudly made their vehicles in this city, but once employed one in every five people living in Michigan.
It was also here that an automotive genius, John DeLorean, was born.

His father, a Romanian immigrant, worked as a union organizer for the Ford Motor Company, but his poor English skills and lack of education restricted him from gaining a higher position in the business.
Whereas from a young age, John DeLorean showed great interest in technology and excelled at his studies.
He got accepted into the Lawrence Institute of Technology, where he turned his attention to industrial engineering.
His future looked bright, but his personal life was getting dark.
During this time, John's parents divorced, and his father would become a reclusive drug addict.
John was then drafted to fight in World War 2 and served three years in the army.
After all this, John realised that although he wanted to pursue engineering, he needed to help his family out, since they were in very poor living conditions.
Thus, John got a job selling life insurance.
It wasn't something he particularly enjoyed, but he did gain a lot of communication skills here that helped him become a great salesman.
John grew bored in the job though, and eventually an opportunity came up for a postgraduate program run by the Chrysler Institute for Automotive Engineers.

After graduating from the program, John was able to join the engineering team of Chrysler, which he then leveraged into getting an even better job at General Motors, initially working in their Pontiac division.
John worked hard, and thanks to the mentors he had at the company, he was soon able to work up to the position of Chief Engineer for Pontiac.
However, John loved European sports cars, especially those made by Enzo Ferrari.
So when he was put in charge of Pontiac, DeLorean decided that America should have their own version of a powerful sports car, and he led the development of the Pontiac GTO.
This was a risk, as the heads of General Motors weren't impressed by the idea and didn't see the point, since they already had powerful fast cars like the Camaro and Corvette.
But John backed himself, and it paid off.
The public loved it, and John got promoted to the head of the Pontiac division, making him the youngest division head at GM at only 40 years old.
John continued making improvements to the GTO, which helped start America's muscle car era.
However, John already had his sights set on his next challenge.
He wanted to make a powerful luxury car.
The problem was, Pontiac didn't have the funds for it.
So John sweet-talked his boss to transfer some funds from another division over to the Pontiac team.
And before long, John had led the development of the Pontiac 1969 Grand Prix car.
Once again, John had taken a risk on a car that many executives didn't think was a good idea, but once again, sales numbers were great, and John had helped boost the brand's reputation.
John DeLorean quickly became a household name, as he started showing up in magazines, televised interviews, and big car events.
His image was helped further, as he was almost the complete opposite of the other Detroit automotive heads.
Whilst they were all elderly men who dressed in black suits with ties, John DeLorean was younger, had long brushed hair, and wore sneakers and open button shirts.
He did things differently and was very charismatic.
And thus, he started to develop an image as a bit of a maverick.
He was also seen at big celebrity parties and often dated famous actresses and models.
In fact, the first time he ever saw his third wife was when he saw her on the cover of a magazine.
GM knew they had a rockstar on their hands and if he could become the face of their development team, then it would help boost sales even further.
So, GM once again promoted John DeLorean and made him the head of their most prized division, Chevrolet.
Now GM was the largest car company in the world at the time, so John was of course thrilled to be rising up the ranks so quickly, however this promotion couldn't have come at a worse moment.
Chevrolet was going through a very rough patch as they were completely behind schedule with their production and facing massive delays, which was allowing competitors to dominate instead.

However, just like he'd done in the Pontiac division, John managed to turn things around for Chevrolet, as he managed to speed up production by simplifying the car designs, as well as lowering assembly costs and improving Chevrolet's reputation.

In truth, John's own personal public image had helped as well, as his cool persona continued to grow, because John was one of the first corporate leaders of the time to be publicly living such an exciting life.
Seeing how well John was boosting car sales, GM then decided to use his fame to sell their new compact family sedan, the Vega.

John went back to his insurance salesman tactics and began touting the Vega as the highest quality product Chevrolet has ever made, and that it could beat any European in car in handling and acceleration.
Both statements proved to be untrue, as the Vega was plagued with engineering, reliability and safety problems.
But despite the crazy statements, Americans bought the Vega largely because John told them to, and over 270,000 were sold.
Before long, John was promoted to Vice President of General Motors, and many thought he would eventually become the president of the whole company.
But this kind of scared GM's executives.
John's eccentricity and unusual style was very unpredictable.
He didn't always do what he was supposed to, and some executives felt his seemingly rock and roll lifestyle didn't give the company the kind of stability an organization like GM needed.
And thus, they began fighting with John over his ideas for the future of GM.
You see, John didn't like having to sell the Vega, and wanted to go back to making cars that excited him.
He wanted to compete against Ferrari GTOs instead of competing against Volkswagen Beetles.
Now, what happened next is still debated.
Some say that after John gave a speech highlighting the company's flaws and publicly outing some executives, GM lost patience with him and forced him out of the company.
Others say John just felt like GM was too corporate and holding him back, and that he was so fed up with having to please the conservative executives that he quit.
Whatever the truth was, John was now out of the company and ready to take on the biggest bet of his career.
For half a century, America didn't really have any new car manufacturers, because to compete with the big three was crazy.
But John DeLorean perhaps was a little crazy, and certainly extremely ambitious.
So John made the risky decision to start his own car company.
With his star power and vast automotive industry connections, in 1973 John created the DeLorean Motor Company, or DMC as it was known.
And John wanted the first DMC car to be a sports car built from the ground up.
Something that could show the world what he would have accomplished at GM if it wasn't for other executives interfering and restricting him.
Something that represented the future.
Something that would change the world.
To do this, John recruited Lotus founder Colin Chapman to design the chassis, and DeLorean designed the body along with Giorgetto Giugiaro, who'd design cars for Ferrari and Alfa Romeo.
John also poached some engineers from GM.
Together, they came up with a futuristic-looking sports car that would come with gullwing doors, a rear engine, and be made with stainless steel.
At the time, many European sports cars were vulnerable to rust since they used thin metals to keep the weight of the car light.
But stainless steel doesn't rust as easily, so it not only gave the car a shiny futuristic look, it also helped protect the car against bad weather.

After assembling the right team and using his automotive contacts to get the different parts he needed, such as an engine that could offer his car the speed and power he wanted, the DMC DeLorean was born as a concept car, which John called the DMC-12.
The problem was, although it was striking to look at, it was still only a concept, and actual production of the car seemed almost impossible, especially with the budget DeLorean had.
But John was a smart salesman, and managed to use his network he'd built up to raise money by selling investors on his vision for the company.
However, to build a manufacturing plant required even more money than he could raise from individual investors, and so he really needed the support of a government.

But the USA, Germany, Italy and Japan, who were all automotive giants, didn't seem to be interested in supporting DeLorean's new company, as they didn't think it would be able to compete with its bigger rivals.
So, John looked at countries that were going through a rough time and desperately needed employment as perhaps they would give him government grants in return for creating jobs.
And there was just one country that was willing to give DeLorean the money needed to open a car factory, and that was Northern Ireland.
The only problem was that meant he'd have to build his business in a war zone.
From the late 1960s to the late 1990s, Ireland had gone through a violent conflict which became known as the Troubles.

Now, this period is too nuanced to properly explain in just a few seconds, but the simplified version is that the Catholics in the country were being discriminated against and denied civil rights, which led to them protesting and a stronger nationalist sentiment starting to grow.
The country became very divided between the Protestants, who mostly wanted to remain part of the United Kingdom, and the Catholics, who didn't.

The UK then sent the military to try and keep the peace in Northern Ireland, but this only made matters worse as it caused many nationalists to feel like they were under attack from Great Britain, leading to the revival of organizations like the Irish Republic Army, or IRA, who viewed the conflict as a guerrilla war for national independence.
Both sides formed their own paramilitaries and lots of fighting broke out.
And thus, you had this situation that was kind of like a civil war, as the country was so divided and political and religious tensions were running very high.
As a result, Northern Ireland quickly became a dangerous and violent place.
There was constant riots, street violence, and even bombings and assassinations became normal.
thousands of lives were lost in this brutal conflict spanning several decades.
Unsurprisingly, not many businesses were looking to invest in the country with all this going on, and thus unemployment in Northern Ireland was very high.
Enter John DeLorean, with his plan to create a new car company that could create lots of jobs and help the economy.

Since the UK government was desperate to try and create some peace between the Protestant and Catholics, and help tackle rising unemployment, they decided to give grants to John DeLorean to help him build a car factory in Northern Ireland from the city of Belfast.
John DeLorean later commented that literally no other country would give him any funding, that they didn't think this company would survive.
But since no new companies really wanted to go to Northern Ireland at the time with all the riots and fighting going on, Northern Ireland was as desperate for jobs as John was desperate for funding.
So the deal worked for both sides.
And despite all the violence and hate going on outside, the DeLorean factory became a peaceful common ground between the Catholic and Protestant workers.
Whilst they fought each other on the streets, inside the factory they worked side by side.
And together, the Iris workers were able to get the first DeLorean off the line in 1981.
Finally, John DeLorean proved to the world that it was possible to start up a car company from scratch and deliver a car that looked like it came from another world.
Unfortunately, the story of DeLorean is not a success story.
Although creating this new car was a great triumph for DeLorean, it didn't mean people were rushing to buy it for several good reasons.
For starters, the DMC-12 was an American car with an Italian design, a mostly French engine, and was built in a factory where none of the workers had any previous car-making experience.
None of those things led to reliability, so the DeLorean was solved full of problems.
Another thing was the price tag.
The DMC DeLorean sold for around $25,000, which is more like $70,000 in today's money.
For context, at the same time, you could buy a Corvette for almost half the price.
Whilst John had wanted to make an affordable car, costs had spiralled out of control.
And as well as being pricey, the car got a bad reputation because the first batch they produced had some engineering and performance issues.
The DeLorean's engine was too weak to power the heavy car, and so the sports car was as slow as a family sedan.
Plus, in 1981, the economy tanked, and nobody was willing to spend an exuberant amount of money on a sports car anyway.
Not only did the economy damage the car industry, it also allowed for Japanese companies to take over the market with cheaper, more reliable alternatives.
And the recession and bad exchange rates also hurt DeLorean even further.
As a result, just a year after the first DMC DeLorean rolled out of the factory line, the DeLorean Motor Company was on the verge of bankruptcy.
But still, John was sure that his car would be a hit, it just needed more time and a few adjustments.
But for that, DeLorean needed even more money.
And unfortunately for John, it was around this time that Margaret Thatcher became Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, and she wanted to significantly reduce government spending.

She felt her predecessors had given DeLorean too much money already, so she immediately ceased all government funding of the factory in Northern Ireland and refused to give John any more money to bail the company out.
Desperate for money and now facing a closure of his one and only manufacturing plant, John needed to raise the money himself and looked for any deal he could get.
John truly cared about his company and wasn't just going to let it die, so he reported he travelled all over the world meeting investors.
But his salesman charm seemed to have run out, as he couldn't convince people DeLorean was a good bet anymore.
Still, John DeLorean vowed to his team that he would find a way to get the money.
But when he said that, nobody could have predicted what he'd do next.
A former neighbour of John's, knowing that he needed money fast, contacted him and told him of a deal that could get him millions of dollars very quickly.
This was exactly what John needed.
The only problem was that the deal involved buying and selling a very large shipment of cocaine.
Feeling like he had no other way to make money to save his company, John agreed to this drug smuggling deal, and a meeting was set in a hotel in Los Angeles near LAX airport.
John was told this deal would make him millions of dollars in total, which he would then use to revive his car company, and thus John agreed to the scheme.
However, this former neighbour of John's was actually setting him up, and was secretly working as an FBI informant to try and reduce a prison sentence he'd received.
And so, the whole thing was a sting operation by the FBI.

And just as they were toasting to the agreement, FBI agents suddenly burst into the room and John was arrested and charged with conspiracy to obtain and distribute 24 million dollars worth of cocaine.
And because the whole thing was a planned setup, they had video evidence of John agreeing to this very illegal deal.
Quite suddenly, John realised that he'd gone from a popular celebrity at the peak of his career to facing serious jail time.
In 1984, after 22 weeks of court proceedings, a surprising verdict was reached.
John DeLorean would not be heading to jail, as during his trial John was able to prove he was a victim of entrapment.
Despite John agreeing to the deal, the jury saw the whole thing as a setup of a desperate man who'd been trying to save his car company.

Now, many believe that the reason the US government had tried to set up John DeLorean was because it would have been a great publicity move for Reagan's war on drugs to prosecute someone who, at the time, was a big name celebrity.
The problem was, the FBI informant had told the FBI that John had suggested the drug deal, when in reality, that was not the case at all, it was very much a setup.
And thus, John DeLorean was found not guilty.
Whilst this was clearly very fortunate for John, the damage had been done.
John DeLorean and his shiny sports car were on the cover of every newspaper and magazine in the country over the scandal.
His name became synonymous with sleazy drug deals.
John DeLorean's reputation, just as his father's, had been destroyed by drugs.
Just in a different way.
John knew his legacy had been tarnished forever.
When a reporter asked him if he would ever return to the car industry, John said, I don't know, would you buy a used car from me?
However, they do say any press is good press, and despite John feeling like his car career was over, all the publicity his trial got meant many people heard about the DeLorean car because of it.
And they started to see it as a cool car with a cool story because of the scandal John had been involved in.
People saw the car next to John's face in newspapers and magazines so much, they started to like the car more than they had initially believed.
Thus, for a short time, DMC sold more DeLoreans than ever before.
But it wasn't enough to keep the factory in Belfast open, so they were forced to shut it down in 1982.
Over a thousand workers were laid off, and in total, only 9,000 DeLoreans were ever actually produced.
The Irish workers protested over the plant's closure for months, but their frustrations never amounted to anything.
The DeLorean Company was dead.
